items.body: Simi Fyda‘s In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn offers no gentle introduction. Compared to Yuri (2023), it works within a noticeably narrower palette. The bright contrasts of its predecessor have given way to a largely monochrome world, built from minute variations of timbre, pressure and pitch. Many of the preoccupations of Yuri remain, but they are pursued with greater concentration. The music repeatedly folds back on itself, testing how much tension can be extracted from the smallest amount of material. The opening track, “-may-care”, signals a state of abrasion, establishing an atmosphere of metallic coldness that hangs over the entire record. “maso chords” introduces a faint current of nostalgia, its harmonies carrying the suggestion of something remembered yet irretrievable. From there, the material grows steadily more compressed. “idle hands” simmers without release, while “hedo chords” circles obsessively around recurring intervals and frozen harmonic figures. By the time “mono chords” arrives, repetition itself has become the subject. Minute tonal inflections slowly reshape the surface until the music seems to trap itself inside its own logic, producing a sense of claustrophobia without ever resorting to excess. Originally conceived as an octophonic installation before being reimagined for stereo, the music acquires an unusually enclosed character. Sounds seem unable to disperse, and repeated gestures linger, each return carrying greater psychological weight. Even the faint vocal traces remain caught within the surrounding texture, surfacing only briefly before dissolving back into the dense harmonic field. The closing “take the hindmost” provides the only substantial shift in perspective. Layers of electronic residue and circuitry redirect attention towards texture itself, as if searching for a new vocabulary from within the material already at hand. Nothing resolves. Instead, the album erases its own traces, leaving behind only the memory of sounds unwilling to disappear. The allow us to delve deeper into her personal heaven, Simi Fyda has kindly agreed to answer four questions by email. The album emerged from what you describe as “a version that almost existed” — music composed during a period of isolation and then reshaped into its final form. Could you talk about what was lost, what was retained, and whether you think traces of that unrealised version still haunt the record we hear today? I started the octophonic pieces during a period where I genuinely couldn’t make anything. I had no access to whatever I normally rely on. So I thought okay, let’s see if I still can do this. It was less of a decision and more just something to do, or to maintain. When I came back to it I was still kinda fed up with the whole thing, which actually helped. I stopped being careful with it and a lot got cut. But the atmosphere stayed, which annoyed me at first because I half wanted a clean break from it. I think that the earlier version is still in there somewhere, not as a foundation, probably more like the thing the record keeps almost touching without quite getting there. You have said that composing this music felt like becoming a demon — specifically one of the figures your grandmother claimed to have encountered in the very space where the album was eventually completed. How did that family story enter the work, and what does the title In My Personal Heaven, I’m the Devil’s Spawn reveal about the relationship between ancestry, memory, and self-transformation in your practice? I moved back into my grandmother’s apartment last November for a couple months and basically just disappeared into it. I wasn’t planning to make a record about any of that. I thought I was making something from a place rather than about it. She had paranoid schizophrenia, periods of seeing figures, demons, specific presences in specific corners of that apartment. I grew up hearing all of it, kind of terrified and fascinated at the same time. I lived there alone as a teenager too. So by the time I came back last november, it was already carrying a lot, I just wasn’t thinking about it consciously. She died in March, right after the album was finished. The timing still felt… I don’t even have a word to use here to be honest. The album isn’t about her, at least that wasn’t the intention. But she’s in there. Much of the album feels remarkably restrained. Tracks seem to hover on the verge of unleashing a full sonic assault, yet repeatedly pull back into themselves. Even the buried vocal traces feel half-suppressed, as though emerging from behind a wall. Was this tension between eruption and containment a conscious compositional strategy, or did it arise naturally from the material? Mostly conscious. I over-anticipate everything. I’ll have already resolved something in my head before it’s even happened, which just kills it. So a lot of this was genuinely trying not to do that. Whenever something felt like it was building toward release I’d just hold it there a bit longer than felt comfortable. I kept reminding myself that circling around something can be enough, that I don’t always have to arrive, don’t have to control every outcome in the ways I’ve conditioned myself to. The record is built around recurrence rather than development, with sounds, intervals, pipe tones and microtonal clusters reappearing in altered forms throughout the album. Given your background in installation and spatial sound, how did the process of collapsing an octophonic work into stereo affect your thinking about repetition, space and listening? Did reducing the physical dimensions of the piece paradoxically make it feel more intimate, claustrophobic, or psychologically charged? The recurrence came from spending a long time with a very small pool of material. At some point development just stopped making sense as a framework. Returning somehow did. In the octophonic versions sound could leave, it had a room to dissolve into. In stereo it couldn’t, so everything that was previously escapable became structural. The noise, the density, all of it just stayed there and then I brought it all even closer and it changed what the material actually was. I think space didn’t disappear, it just stopped being outside the work.

items._cn_summary: Simi Fyda 的《In My Personal Heaven, I'm the Devil's Spawn》从一张多元色彩的专辑收窄至近乎单色的声响世界，以微妙的音色、张力与音高变化构建压迫感。作品最初为八声道环绕声装置创作，后改编为立体声版本，使声音呈现出异常封闭、内敛的特质。重复手法成为核心议题，反复出现的音程与冻结的和声碎片将听众困于音乐自身的逻辑之中，形成幽闭恐惧式的密度。人声痕迹仅在织体中短暂浮现，随即消融。终曲转向电子残响与线路感，以材质本身作为新词汇的源头。专辑拒绝解决与释放，最终抹去自身痕迹，仅留下不愿消散的声音记忆。这种封闭、自反的实验取向与深度声音探索，与偏好实验、前卫与电子音乐的听众高度契合。

items.body: Listening to “adventurous” music can be a hazardous activity. It often prompts a familiar question from unsuspecting visitors: “What is this noise?” toppe bianche 白色补丁 by Li Song / Luciano Maggiore begins precisely at that point of uncertainty, asking not only how one should listen to a work, but whether listening can ever be separated from the circumstances in which it takes place. Recorded beneath the railway arches and across the marshes of Walthamstow, London, the album functions as a negotiation between portable electronics, passing trains, weather, wildlife, and human activity. Consisting of two long-form mirror pieces, “/ * /” and “* / *“, the album is built around simple materials: glissandi, friction-like textures, environmental sounds, and interludes of white noise. The title, which translates as “White Patches”, refers to the masking processes used in post-production and the way the different sounds are connected. Trains become white noise, while birdsong, distant conversations, footsteps and accidental events drift in and out of focus. As the artists themselves insist, there is no background here. Everything is present all the time. What soon becomes apparent is the way toppe bianche 白色补丁 refuses to privilege any single element. The portable speakers generating the glissandi are no more important than the arch itself, the trains overhead, or the occasional passer-by. The music exists in a state between composition and improvisation, intention and accident. The sounds feel fragile, yet stubbornly present. They neither demand attention nor disappear entirely. For those not having a tape deck, headphones might reveal the intricate layering of the recording. Personally, I feel the album especially rewarding when played through my laptop speakers in an ordinary domestic environment especially on hot summer days. With windows open, street noise, birds outside, distant traffic, even the hum of household appliances become inadvertent extensions of the piece. In this sense, Toppe Bianche is not simply a recording but a framework for listening. Like the cliché of the tree falling in the forest, it raises questions about perception and presence. The glissandi may occasionally vanish beneath trains, white noise or the sounds of one’s own surroundings, but they continue to exist. That quiet insistence may be the album’s most radical gesture. In the following interview conducted by email Li Song and Luciano Maggiore elaborate on the production process. Li Song and Luciano Maggiore This recording was made beneath the railway arches and across the marshes of Walthamstow, with passing trains becoming an integral part of the sound world. Rather than attempting to isolate yourselves from the environment, you chose to add white noise and work with it. How did the location shape the music, and at what point did the surrounding sounds cease to be “background” and become collaborators in the piece? Luciano Maggiore: The simple fact that we chose to use that arch in the marshes says a lot about how much we wanted the recording to be entangled with the place. It’s a place we both know quite well, having been the location of a small, almost spontaneous festival of experimental music organised by a few friends and us some years ago. The main characters in the work are, of course, the sounds produced by us during the acts of recording and post-production, but the flesh of the pieces, and the world they inhabit, is that arch itself, with its inhabitants and all the accidents imposed by the surrounding sonic life. There is no background. Everything is present all the time. Li Song: Both Luciano and I are quite familiar with the space itself. A couple of years back, the two of us and some friends did an outdoor show under the exact same arch. We both live near the marshes but in opposite directions, so I wouldn’t be surprised if the arch is actually the midpoint between our homes in London. When we decided to record outdoors, that was the first space that came to mind. I think the location sort of designed the piece, in a way we didn’t expect it to at the start. We had chatted about the idea of masking very early on, which is putting one audio signal on top of another to cover it up. But then we sort of forgot about it and went down the route of recording glissandos under the arch. Later on, while working with the recordings, the idea came back to us. The white noise masking, around and over with the train, holds the pieces together. The album is described as existing between composition and improvisation, and between human dialogue and environmental processes. Can you talk about how decisions were made during the recording? Were there agreed structures, or did the piece emerge through listening and reacting to each other, the trains, and the acoustics of the space? LM: The pieces had a backbone that was decided a priori: the use of glissandos, a series of movements through the space, and a range of frequencies we could work with in both pieces. Decisions were then made in situ, following recording attempts and small trials and errors, to understand whether the choices made beforehand suited the situation we found ourselves in. I would say the core idea was to use digital glissandos and, later, fields of white noise to mask certain parts of the recordings. Li Song built a simple piece of software that was easy to control, with an array of parameters (frequency and duration, if I remember correctly). We performed with the software using our phones, each connected to an identical Bluetooth speaker. LS: If I remember correctly, we only had the moving glissando idea and the location planned out. We left pretty much everything else to the day of the recording. Both of us are quite flexible and just open to seeing what happens. I had programmed an oscillator app on a webpage so we could use our portable speakers to generate the glissando sounds. That’s the continuous sound you hear in the recordings, where you can change the pitch range and certain timing settings. On the day, I showed Luciano how to use it, and we briefly talked about how we would move around the space. We did maybe two or three sessions with different settings and configurations. I feel like as we recorded the latter half, we started improvising more and ignoring the rules we had set at the beginning. After that, we just went home to listen back and work on it later. It was during that later process that we had the masking idea with white noise to go along with the train sounds. It didn’t take us long to find an alternative way to mask the other track, and I think the two tracks work better together. Li, your work with No Performance often seeks to minimise the presence of the performer, while Luciano’s practice frequently examines performance itself, repetition, endurance and the theatricality of sound production. How did these seemingly different approaches interact during this collaboration? Did either of you find yourselves working outside your usual habits? LM: Even though our approaches may appear different, both of us perform in various formations that use performativity as a way of staging situations involving sound. Li Song often performs with the artist Mengting Zhuo, and both of us are part of a trio with On Yee Lo, among other collaborations. I would say that neither of us felt in any way out of place LS: The ‘No Performance’ idea actually started out as a series of experiments that Zhu Wenbo and I were doing in Beijing back in 2015. We were doing pieces where the computer listened to acoustic instruments and did its own thing according to the program we had designed beforehand. It was maybe a half-joke to name it ‘No Performance’ because I would just start the program and sit there doing nothing. To be honest, we eventually explored other ideas beyond this style. So it’s not some strict rule I follow throughout all my music. Having said that, I do feel I have grown more attached to the idea of letting things perform by ‘themselves.’ I do believe that somehow shows in this music too. Maybe you could say the different approaches work in different dimensions. I think our approaches overlap more than what it looks like. The liner notes mention a desire to create a music that “eschews self-awareness in favour of a supernatural imbalance.” That is a striking phrase. What does “supernatural imbalance” mean to you in this context? Is it connected to unpredictability, to the agency of the environment, or to a more philosophical idea of dissolving control? LM: That’s a beautiful way of describing the work, but we can’t really claim ownership of the phrase. I think I understand what Cai and Yizhuo (the owners of Aloe) are implying with it, but I would rather leave any explanation to them. LS: To me, my first impression when hearing the track after we add the studio material was actually a sense of balance. Just like the album title, the patch holds things together. Listening to the album, there are moments where it becomes difficult to distinguish between performer, device, environmental sound and recording artefact. Both of your practices seem interested in questioning authorship and intentionality. Do you see this blurring of boundaries as a political gesture, an aesthetic one, or simply the most honest way of engaging with sound today? LM: I’m not sure about honesty. I don’t personally think of what I do as particularly political. There are, of course, other, more effective ways of making a statement than using music to do so. I’m conscious that every position I take in this world carries political value and therefore implies a certain stance. However, I am concerned with music making and the ways in which it can be staged. I believe in making music for music’s sake. LS: I think this is just naturally how we work. With computer or electronic music, there’s a huge appreciation for high-fidelity audio and how many channels you have in your system. For me, ever since my time in Beijing, I’ve performed with my laptop in people’s living rooms, playing through a bunch of cheap small speakers I found for 30 RMB each on Taobao. Not everyone has access to a 16-channel speaker system, and more importantly, there’s just music for laptop speakers. Luciano and I also worked together on the ‘unspecified unspecified unspecified’ concert series in London for a year after COVID. We had this rule of self-amplification, where performers were solely responsible for amplifying their own sound if they needed to. I suppose that’s also related to this idea: people working with their own things, in the space they are given. What is the significance of the title toppe bianche 白色补丁? LM: The Italian toppe bianche can be roughly translated into English as “white patches”. I believe that 白色补丁 is read and understood in more or less the same way. LS: I already referred to title holding things in the above answers, it matches what we were doing with the studio material in the end. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body:
The previous Ezz-thetics column reflected the near-simultaneous appearance of three works of individual brilliance, solo recordings by Liz Allbee, Hannah Marshall, and John Butcher. In the months since, three mid-size, improvisation-rich ensembles, drawing inspiration from more or less explicit environmental themes have appeared, with varying degrees of composition and improvisation, led by musicians of comparable vision: Magda Mayas, Pascal Niggenkemper, and Marta Warelis.

Each is characterized by different degrees of copyright participation, signalling contrasting relations of composition and improvisation. Magda Mayas’ Filamental’s Murmur, evidently as collective as a murmuration of starlings, is copyrighted in the names of all eight musicians. Pascal Niggenkemper’s d’une rive a l’autre is largely copyrighted to the composer/bassist, 11 of the 17 tracks, with six tracks credited to improvised duets from the eight instrumentalists of the Ensemble Tuvalu. Marta Warelis’s Still Life with Lemons is largely credited to the leader/composer. All recently released, the three come from a specific moment in time, the autumn of 2024: Murmur was recorded in Berlin in September; Still Life with Lemons in Amsterdam in October; d’une rive a l’autre in Berlin in November.

Magda Mayas’ Filamental’s Murmur (Relative Pitch) is an octet with a strong emphasis on strings in its make-up; as well as the leader’s piano, there are two harpists, Zeena Parkins and Rhodri Davies, pretty much covering the terrain of free improvising harpists; two cellists, Aimée Theriot-Ramos and Anthea Caddy; two reeds, alto saxophonist Christine Abdelnour and clarinetist Michael Thieke, and violinist Angharad Davies. Murmur is a singular piece, almost 38 minutes long.

There are few spectacles as emblematic of collective mind as a murmuration of starlings, thousands of birds joined in extraordinary aerobatic maneuvers that mock the reckless waste, noise, and danger of fighter jet ballets. Part of the special genius of Magda Mayas’ Filamental is that it never sounds anything like what one might expect from its string-heavy personnel. Everything is sublimated into quiet percussive events, a music that suggests the sublime piety of chance events in nature, like a light rain on large leaves. Hence, Mayas’ description of the work:

I am fascinated by the coordination and elegance of a flock of birds flying, forming beautiful murmurations, constantly changing, seemingly without effort. This communal act provides protection through the sheer number of birds and their changing position; it is an exchange of information amongst them, and it has a clear collective ending when the flock decides to fly back to the ground.

In Murmur, I want to explore how a large ensemble can make use of these instincts of communal movement, coordination, shape shifting and, eventually, potential simultaneous endings through distinct decisions around material and structure but also shared memories of events that were created together.

The doubling of instruments will lend a certain anonymity to the music, furthered by the frequency of isolated percussive details, whether a sustained note from Abdenour suggests a bowed string instrument, or cellos and/or violin are used for a maze of quarter tones. It’s the very nature of the murmuration that will define this collective composition, hive mind or flock consciousness, yes, some overriding shared awareness, existence, and impulse. With no dedicated percussionist present (depending on how you might classify the piano), this is frequently percussion music of the highest order, struck strings on piano and string instruments create a bevy of string-drum plosives. The collective act itself is essentially harmonious in its nature, the special transparency of string harmonics creating a sonic window that opens onto the Cagean silence of the entire ensemble. The cumulative experience is of an interior soundscape in art channeled through the piano and taking place both in the octet and in the listener. A rare and beautiful sonic act.

Pascal Niggenkemper’s Ensemble Tuvalu’s d’une rive a l’autre (Subran 07) is inspired by Tuvalu, the Polynesian archipelago that is currently set to disappear below the Pacific’s waves in a few decades, a paradisical world doomed by climate change. As with Mayas’ Murmur, the bassist/composer’s ensemble is an octet, made up of instrumental pairings: Ben LaMar Gay’s cornet with Louis Lorain’s trumpet; Mona Matbou Riahi’s clarinet with Joachim Badenhorst’s; Tizia Zimmermann’s accordion with that of Artemis Vavatsika’s; Niggenkemper’s double bass paired, less precisely, with Elisabeth Coudoux’s cello. Each of the musicians will also have a vocal role, singing, chanting, or reciting, and Jaumes Privat will appear near the end of the work for an extended spoken word passage.

In her expansive liner note, Julia Neupert, cites the composer’s overarching concerns here:

Niggenkemper is interested in how differently people are shaped – culturally, socially, emotionally – not only in musical terms. He is concerned with broadening perspectives, recognizing other points of view, and collective thinking and creation. In this way, the project also reflects a central cultural value of Tuvaluan society: “Kaitasi” – the principle of always shaping one’s own life in connection with the community. An idea that could hardly be more relevant in our time.

d’une rive a l’autre is a work of daunting complexity. In a “live” staging, drums and metal discs are center stage; a series of 16 sound curtains of plastic and metal with exciter resonators activated by foot pedals surround the stage. All the musicians sing and speak traditional Tuvaluan songs and poems as well as singing freely adapted poems drawn from multiple languages. It comes as both a CD and a DVD. The CD was recorded over four days in the Südwestrundfunk Baden-Baden studio. It has 17 tracks and represents something like the totality of the audio work. The DVD was recorded with an audience in the Tollhaus Karlsruhe a day later. It has 12 tracks, is significantly shorter, sacrifices the instrumental duets, but is enriched by sheer theatrical intensity. Either way, it’s stellar work, with Niggenkemper’s insistence on a humane art reflecting both human potential and the necessity of engaging our collective condition with work of special power. The multiple demands that he places on his musicians are answered with stunning results in the additional tracks on the studio recordings, reflecting the brief individual duets among the matched instruments.

The DVD performance was also presented on the Free Jazz Blog at the time of its release, and it remains available online. It’s an immediate introduction to the work’s combination of visceral emotional power and often luminous instrumental textures:

https://www.freejazzblog.org/2025/03/pascal-niggenkempers-tuvalu-ensemble.html

Marta Warelis’s Still Life with Lemons (Relative Pitch) may be less immediately shaped by environmental concerns than the preceding, but lyric ideas of landscape and the impress of environment still figure in her compositions, from “Birds” to “The Sky Blushes Sunset” to “Ashes to Sea.” The group is a multi-national sextet, with the Polish pianist/synthesist Warelis joined by Hollander Ab Baars, clarinet, tenor saxophone; Canadian Karen Ng, clarinet, alto saxophone; Norwegian Ingebrigt Håker Flaten, double bass; and Americans Ben LaMar Gay, trumpet and electronics and Frank Rosaly drums and gongs. That might suggest a forceful, wind-driven ensemble, but the emphasis is reflective, intimate, sometimes pensive, often witty. Thin instrumental textures predominate, sometimes with different instruments’ sounds penetrating one another, even creating beat patterns as pitches approach one another.

The opening “Birds” begins with an extended solo piano passage immediately emphasizing a certain intimacy. It will persist as the horns enter, with significant dissonance, in a slow interweaving of instrumental voices, ultimately matching the longing of the winds’ theme against the chaotic rush of Warelis and the rhythm section. “There to the Bridge,” an Albanian folk song, receives a plaintively nostalgic performance with Gay setting the mood before the two clarinetists carry the mournful theme to its furthest reaches. The band possesses genuine wit, as apparent in “Alternate Endings,” continuously propelled by Warelis and Håker Flaten’s broken rhythms, effectively extended by the flaring tone of Gay’s trumpet and the dense squawking supplied by Baars’ tenor saxophone. “Intermittent Web of Sorts” proceeds from the initially hesitant patterns of Håker Flaten and Rosaly before Warelis and Gay introduce the theme, textures gradually accumulating. It ultimately reaches an accumulation of sustained winds and electronics, pitches sliding in and out of beat patterns, a high point in the music’s special interconnectedness.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦于2024年秋三支中型即兴乐团的专辑：Magda Mayas领衔的八重奏、Pascal Niggenkemper的Ensemble Tuvalu、以及Marta Warelis的Still Life with Lemons。评论深入剖析了即兴与作曲之间的版权分配差异，以及不同乐手在集体创作中的角色。Mayas的作品受椋鸟群飞启发，八件乐器以弦乐为主却呈现出打击乐般的颗粒质感，音乐通过共享的结构决策实现即兴中的协调与突变。Niggenkemper的十七首作品中既有作曲框架也有六首即兴二重奏。Warelis则更偏向领导者作曲。整体体现了欧洲自由即兴场景对自然主题、结构探索与集体意识的持续关注。

items.body:
Over the course of the last decade, the group أحمد [Ahmed] has carved out a distinctive approach to the jazz canon through their tireless exploration of the music of Ahmed Abdul-Malik. Mining Abdul-Malik’s compositions and his incorporation of non-Western microtonality into the jazz vocabulary, pianist Pat Thomas, alto saxophone player Seymour Wright, bassist Joel Grip, and drummer Antonin Gerbal have done more than reinterpretation. They have used the music as a foundation for both immersion and subversion of the way that the standard jazz quartet functions within post-bop structures. For last year’s Sama'a (Audition), they went into the studio for an expansive refraction of Abdul-Malik’s Jazz Sahara. During that same session, the four took a slight detour to record Play Monk, a dive into deconstructions of six pieces by Thelonious Monk, all but one of which he recorded in the late 1950s when Abdul-Malik was part of his group. أحمد [Ahmed] has incorporated Monk tunes into their live sets but this is the first time they have focused on his tunes on a recording.

While Thomas, Wright, Grip, and Gerbal have not altered their strategies in the switch of source material, there is one significant shift in the way one listens to this music. A quick search returns no other versions of Abdul-Malik’s pieces other than those recorded by the composer or أحمد [Ahmed] whereas Monk’s “Epistrophy” or “’Round Midnight” have hundreds. Even a less well-known piece like “Oska T” has dozens. Because the pieces covered are so well known, their teasing apart and restructuring of the underlying thematic kernels are more readily evident. Over two CDs, the quartet digs in, with improvisations that range between 20 and 30 minutes with the exception of a seven-minute extrapolation of “Epistrophy.” These extended explorations allow the group to excavate the forms with a focused patience, zeroing in on and elucidating microscopic details, extricating them into the fundamental elements of penetrating improvisations.

The first phrases of the opening “Bye-ya / Epistrophy” provide a glimpse of what is to come. Bass and piano circle around the theme and Gerbal’s lithe drumming circles up to drive momentum. Wright’s stabbing alto picks apart the melody and the four launch off on a circuitous inquiry, dismantling Monk’s tune into its constituent fragments and then reassembling them with constructivist abstraction. Each of the four seize on elements of the underlying piece, playing them off of each other with unwavering resolve, an approach the group continues to advance in their sweeping live sets. There is an insistent intensity as Wright’s notes pick and prod at Thomas’ skewed clusters, Grip’s free walking lines, and Gerbal’s churning free rhythms. Shards of “Epistrophy” are introduced into the mix by Grip and Thomas, slowly accruing with multifaceted erudition.

The group continues to subvert expectations with “Friday the Thirteenth” as Thomas insistently repeats the first phrase of the tune against Grip’s growling arco inversions. Wright’s keypad pops and Gerbal’s open percussion build momentum and Wright unleashes spattered honks that open into a collective four-part splintering of the theme, picking it apart and recasting it with angular exactitude, building density and intensity over the course of the sweeping 26-minute improvisation. “’Round Midnight” gets a relatively straightforward introduction with Wright intoning the theme over sinuous bass and cymbal splashes. Thomas’ spare chords enter as the quartet dynamically transposes the constituent parts of the piece with imperturbable resolution resolving with the riveting cycling hushed snare abrasions that brings the piece to a close.

A seven-minute scorching, stuttering run through “Epistrophy” serves as an interlude to an abstracted, cascading reading of “Evidence” which takes Monk’s stop-start theme and explodes it with relentless, spiraled piano phrases and the hurtling momentum of bass and drums driving Wright’s coruscating alto which prods and jabs with spiky dexterity. The 30-minute improvisation is an engulfing exemplification of unflagging invention. Monk’s “Oska T.,” structured around an obsessively cyclical riff, is a fitting conclusion to the release. The quartet slows things down to a free shuffle with bass and alto arcing over the mutable pulse of piano and drums. The four players adroitly weave their lines in and out of the collective undercurrent with indefatigable ingenuity. While others have dedicated themselves to the reinterpretation of the music of Thelonious Monk, أحمد [Ahmed]’s Play Monk is distinctive in its mastery, fully absorbing his music into the collective rigor and artistry of this singular ensemble.

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body: Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Force and sweetness intertwined Operational Ambivalence by Somatic Responses   Brothers John and Paul Healy have been operating as Somatic Responses out of Ammanford, a small industrial mining community in southwest Wales, since 1994. They formed in the hardcore acid techno scene, releasing their first material in 1995 before gradually expanding into industrial, drum and bass, noise, ambient, and breakcore territory. Their 1999 debut Circumflex on Hymen Records was a pivotal moment—taking their sound into new levels of complexity and intensity, and subsequent releases on Ad Noiseam, Sublight, Component, and their own Photon Emissions label built one of the most expansive and underappreciated catalogs in hard-edged electronic music. Key influence on rhythmic noise, breakcore, and IDM, yet somehow always operating just below the mainstream radar. The duo describe their work as “complex dislocated and broken beats, distorted intelligent constructions, fascinating sonic structures, force and sweetness intertwined.” Operational Ambivalence, it’s worth noting, credits “Everything by J.S.Healy“—making this a solo John Healy production, recorded in the Macro Chamber in Ammanford, rather than a full duo effort. The distinction is subtle but real. What you get with Operational Ambivalence is largely what you’d expect from the Somatic Responses catalog: distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout. It’s a 14-track self-released collection that feels like a gathering of material that belongs together rather than a concept album with a rigid arc. Tracks 8, 9, and 14 are the more ambient pieces of the release and still create beautiful visual imagery through technique. Out of that ambient batch, “H doesn’t fall down the stairs…” is the most interesting—not strictly ambient like the other two, but considerably softer in production than everything surrounding it. The lightness and strange composition here is compelling in its subtlety, drum rhythm play with light percussion and glitched patterns that sit between experimental and delicate. Distortion, drums, hectic patterns with beautiful ambience woven throughout :: “New Shift” is another standout, with its intro of rolling clicks and sounds moving left to right across the stereo field, slowly manipulated kick drums coming in gradually as the track builds rhythm. What you thought was a softer track reveals itself as something larger entirely. The technique of building anticipation through percussion here is notable, it recalls the way Lexaunculpt constructed his pattern builds of glitches and various percussions on The Blurring of Trees (Planet Mu, 2003), that same slow accumulation of rhythmic detail until the structure reveals itself. The patterns here are interesting and the execution is patient. “Gatch” is another standout in all of its distortion and drumming. What makes it work compositionally is how it messes with pattern recognition, introducing drum patterns that redirect where you expect the track to go. The distortion is toned down carefully, which is harder than it sounds. Somatic Responses have always been comfortable in distortion’s territory, and John Healy demonstrates that comfort here, using strong distortion without making ears bleed, keeping it controlled enough that it serves the composition rather than overwhelming it. Using strong distortion without making ears bleed :: “Vital Ex Parts 1 and 2” earns its nine-minute runtime—two parts that feel like one extended piece assembled well. The drums in the introduction are playful before they introduce harsher builds, eventually transforming into something darker with ambient surroundings closing in. And “Residual Behaviour” is the track that’s hardest not to stop at simply because of how oddly it stands out in the context of everything else. Real drum samples playing in broken patterns with chords filling in the background—it sounds off, but there’s a strange beauty to it. The double hits, the stutters, the subtle chords and notes behind the rhythm, there’s no steady pulse here, just experimentation. When a rhythm starts forming it plays briefly before switching again, until the track ends on skips and rolls and hi-hats leading the outro with swishy drums. It sounds like it was a genuinely fun track to make, and that energy comes through in the listening. Somatic Responses and John Healy, specifically on this release, have spent over three decades refining the specific space between force and sweetness that their catalog occupies. Operational Ambivalence doesn’t reinvent that space. It just inhabits it with the kind of confidence that comes from thirty years of knowing exactly where you live. Artwork once again by Mattia Travaglini, whose visual language has become as much a part of the Somatic Responses aesthetic as the music itself. Operational Ambivalence is available on Bandcamp. Operational Ambivalence by Somatic ResponsesThe post Somatic Responses :: Operational Ambivalence (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Somatic Responses核心成员John Healy独立完成，延续了该组合三十年来在力度与柔美之间的探索定位。十四首曲目并非严格的概念专辑架构，更像是相互呼应的素材集合：扭曲的鼓组、密集的断拍与穿插其间的环境氛围构成主体，而第八、九、十四轨偏向氛围化处理，以细腻的技法营造视觉化的声场。其中最值得关注的是《H doesn't fall down the stairs...》，它在整体强硬质感中呈现出克制的轻盈感，光滑的轻打击乐与故障化节奏形成微妙的张力。《New Shift》则以滚动的咔哒声开场，立体声场中左右移动的声像逐渐引入踢鼓，揭示出从柔和到宏大结构的渐进逻辑。整体制作延续了Somatic Responses对节奏解构与声音密度的执着，是一份扎实而沉稳的工业电子输出。

items.body: Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. A producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next Kine 3 by Roel Funcken   The golden era of IDM left behind a particular kind of silence, not the absence of music, but the absence of the restless, process-driven curiosity that made that era feel alive. What’s left of it now echoes through the electronic music landscape in small signals, from old and new artists working in the margins. Roel Funcken has been one of those signals for over two decades, and Kine 3 is his loudest transmission yet—a massive tracklist, a substantial runtime, and the third installment of an ongoing series that began as a way of making sense of a large body of work. The Kine series, released through EC Underground—the South Florida-based multidisciplinary collective and label that has been bridging European and UK electronic music to US audiences since 2018, operates on a process-first logic: raw, modular, driven by hardware and intention rather than polish and structure. My first encounter with Roel‘s work came through a college radio station playing Funckarma‘s Part 3 EP on Djak-Up-Bitch, the Rotterdam-based Dutch label specializing in modern electronica and IDM distributed through Clone. That particular series was something, the melodic play and drum work had a freshness that aged remarkably well, still sounds lovely today. Fast forward years later and here we land with Kine 3. This album shows the maturity of Roel as a solo artist, distinct from the Funckarma project that first put him on the map alongside his brother Don. His productions here aren’t built around melodic composition in the conventional IDM sense, they’re explorative and experimental, each track following a particular pattern of letting effects and drums do the talking while atmospheric or melodic backgrounds grind immersively in the background. The loop continues :: With a tracklist this expansive, the best approach is to section it. Tracks 1 through 8 share similarities in style and composition — drums and effects leading, melodies surfacing immersively rather than announcing themselves. What Funcken does here shouldn’t be misread as pure improvisation. It’s closer to freeplay with intention, a distinction that matters. Modular synthesis and process-driven production naturally produce moments that feel unplanned, but behind every patch decision is a set of deliberate choices: which modules are connected, what triggers what, where the randomness is allowed and where it’s controlled. Funcken‘s approach on Kine 3 sits in that exact space—the results sound alive and unpredictable but the architecture holding them together is clearly considered. Track 9, “4ehmth,” functions as a divider. It’s the only track of the bunch that’s almost entirely drum play, and whether intentional or not, it creates a natural break between the first and second halves of the album. “Bydow 32” carries a distinct Funckarma feeling—a reminiscence of “Atomic” or “Finsbury Park” from Part 3, those same loose, melodic textures surfacing again through a different production context. “Dorphins” is another standout. Its melodic structure separates itself from the rest of the batch because the tweaking of the melody is being granularized at fast speeds, bouncing on a single note with harsh portamento bend stabs cutting through. Portamento—the gliding between pitches rather than jumping discretely, becomes a compositional tool here rather than just an effect. When applied fast and aggressively, it creates a pitch tension that sits between melody and noise, which is exactly what Funcken is exploiting. The drum structure across all these tracks is consistently loose and abrasive, not a loop so much as one long continuous rhythm that plays through rather than repeating. The two bonus digital tracks round things out distinctly. “Koidz” is heavier—distorted drums, more rhythmically aggressive than the core album, with a crunchy acid bass and what sounds like significant knob movement throughout. The emotional pads that come in give it a melodic tone that sticks to the structure as it plays, a ringing atmospheric pad leading the melody in a way the main album rarely does. “Kido” takes the same sound palette and reconfigures it—a different melodic composition built from similar material but toned differently, another take on the same logic but with its own feel of rhythm and structure. Kine 3 is a newer sound built off the classic. Roel Funcken has described the Kine series as emerging from a need to process a large body of work—dividing material into categories, finding what felt raw and process-driven and unfinished in the best possible way. He noted that sitting back and listening to Kine 1 with an audience changed something: the distance it created meant he was actually listening rather than judging. The support those releases received went straight back into the system—new Eurorack modules, extending the loop. Kine 3 is what that loop sounds like three iterations in, and it sounds exactly like what it is: a producer still genuinely curious about what his machines will do next, documenting the results with the confidence of someone who’s been doing this long enough to know when to get out of the way and let the process speak. EC Underground found the right home for it. The loop continues. Kine 3 is available on EC Underground. items._cn_summary: 《Kine 3》是荷兰制作人Roel Funcken第三部个人专辑，通过南佛罗里达地下厂牌EC Underground发行。整张专辑体量庞大，延续Kine系列"过程驱动"的创作逻辑，以模块化合成器和硬件为核心，强调原始质感而非后期打磨。Funcken将大量素材按类别整理，从中筛选出最粗粝、最具实验性的部分结集出版。作品中鼓机与效果器主导前景，旋律和氛围层作为沉浸式背景渐次浮现，介于即兴与意图之间——表面听来充满随机感，实则每个模块连接、触发关系和随机性控制都经过深思熟虑。前八首延续同一美学路线，第九首"4ehmth"开始转折。乐评特别指出此作标志着他从早年Funckarma二人组项目中的旋律化IDM路线，演进为以探索性和实验性为核心的成熟个人语汇，与九十年代末IDM黄金时代的"不安好奇心"精神一脉相承。

items.body: Review by blessed_of — Compassionizer tribute to Depeche Mode is a sincere and beautifully crafted homage that captures the emotional depth and melodic power of the original songs, while reimagining them through the band's unique avant-prog and ambient sensibility. Instead of simply reproducing familiar material, Compassionizer opens new dimensions?experimenting with texture, rhythm, and atmosphere to make each piece feel newly discovered. "But Not Tonight" opens the album with a warm, dreamy atmosphere. Where Depeche Mode's version glows with youthful melancholy, Compassionizer transforms it into a reflective meditation. "World Full of Nothing" and "The Things You Said" follow with chamber-like arrangements and subtle electronics, preserving the emotional fragility of the originals while reframing them through the band's layered and expressive sound. "Blue Dress" maintains the sensual minimalism of Depeche Mode but becomes more introspective and ethereal, while "Sibeling" expands into a sweeping ambient dialogue between piano, clarinet, and electronic textures. The closing "Enjoy the Silence" stands not as a cover but as a reimagining?slower, sacred, and contemplative. Where Depeche Mode's originals thrive on sleek synth- pop precision, Compassionizer adds warmth, introspection, and organic depth, creating not imitation but an honest conversation across time and genres. A beautiful, thoughtful, and deeply moving album.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是向Depeche Mode致敬的作品，但不是简单的翻唱。乐队以先锋前卫和氛围电子的独特视角重新诠释原作，在织体、节奏与氛围上展开全新维度。《But Not Tonight》从原作的青春忧郁转化为沉思冥想；《World Full of Nothing》与《The Things You Said》采用室内乐式编曲与微妙的电子元素；《Blue Dress》保留原作的感官极简主义却更为内省空灵；《Sibeling》则扩展为钢琴、单簧管与电子织体间的广阔氛围对话；终曲《Enjoy the Silence》放慢节奏，呈现出庄严而冥想的仪式感。整体以温暖的器乐质感、有机纵深取代原作的合成器流行冷冽精度，跨越时代与流派形成一场真诚的对话。

items.body: The work of Finnish hyper-accordionist Kimmo Pohjonen has never been reviewed on this site. He comes from Finnish folk music but has revolutionized how it sounds, is played, and looks. Pedals and effects augment his accordion, and his own wordless vocals, and it sounds like a mini-orchestra. Pohjonen looks like a modern-day pagan shaman who moves with ecstatic dances and feels at home whether he plays with Kronos Quartet, French jazz drummer Eric Echampard or in the art-rock band KTU (alongside King Crimson alums drummer Pat Mastelotto and Touch guitarist Trey Gunn). Swedish reed and electronics player Mats Gustafsson, like Pohjonen, is an adventurous, inimitable iconoclast who enjoys turning genres inside out like others do their pockets. He comes from punk rock and free jazz, but just look at his new collaborative projects from last year - the surf rock meets free jazz, The MagNuts (with guitarist Hedvig Mollestad), death metal meets free jazz, Backgrillen, and the free-improv flute duo, Flöjter, with French Delphine Joussein (of Nout trio), that already produced two live albums. The musical union of Pohjonen and Swedish reed and electronics player Mats Gustafsson was envisioned by Bogdan Benigar, the director of Druga Godba festival in Ljubljana in Slovenia, who invited both of them to the 2024 edition of the festival, without letting them know that this was his plan. Gustafsson and Pohjonen bonded instantly. They share a love for ice hockey and saunas, and are motivated by a great passion - for spontaneous, risk-taking improvisations, creating a community, and cultivating individual and collective consciousness (as Gustafsson says: fighting against local and global stupidities). Throughout their live performances, they sounded like a powerful, raw, and intense sonic entity, Kimmats, and often Gustafsson’s saxes are channelled through Pohjonen’s effects. Two Balls are Enough is the debut album of Pohjonen and Gustafsson, and it was recorded in a two-day session in Vienna in February 2026 by Martin Siewart (of Radian), with Pohjonen and Gustafsson responsible for the mix. Gustafsson brought to the recording session slide, tenor, baritone and bass saxes, Ab clarinet, flute and slide flute, live electronics, harmonica and organ, while Pohjonen played his electro-acoustic accordion and sang. Each of the nine pieces sends you into unpredictable, uncompromising, deeply visceral, and wonderful hyperactive territories. Club dance pulse on steroids collides with ecstatic free jazz sax blows. Noisy electronics join a cathartic pagan dance, with Pohjonen’s organ-like chords ascending from hell to dance with Gustafsson’s garrulous baritone sax patterns. A poetic cinematic vision of a snowy Arctic storm. Experimenting with feedback-filled, mutated timbres. A touching, singable folk song. Three pieces were inspired by French poet Danielle Collobert. The last piece, “Backgrillen”, sketches a completely different texture from Gustafsson’s death jazz band, and offers a surprisingly intimate, touching melody filled with rustic beauty. It sounds like these Nordic wolves found a new pack of like-minded partner who enjoy creating a genre of their own. Two Balls Are Enough by Mats Gustafsson / Kimmo Pohjonen Email This BlogThis! items._cn_summary: 芬兰手风琴家Kimmo Pohjonen与瑞典萨克斯/电子乐演奏家Mats Gustafsson的合作专辑，由斯洛文尼亚Ljubljana音乐节策展人牵线促成。Pohjonen以电声手风琴配合效果器与无词人声，形成类似迷你管弦乐团的声响体系；Gustafsson则带来多种萨克斯、笛类与口琴，音色常被导入Pohjonen的效果链。九首作品均围绕即兴展开，融合俱乐部舞曲脉动与自由爵士爆发，嘈杂电子与异教仪式感并置，部分作品取材自法国诗人Danielle Collobert的文本意象。整体呈现两位演奏家在即兴框架内对音色、节奏与文化语汇的跨界重组，是欧洲地下即兴场景中具有代表性的合作成果。

items.body: Digital Factor was founded more than 30 years ago, yet the project led by Mike Langer shows no signs of losing momentum. On the contrary, it continues to surprise and evolve. For this new album, Gwendolyn Gaffa officially joins the lineup, contributing to a concept inspired by the creative spirit of 80s New-Wave. It would be unfair to dismiss this as a mere imitation of ’80s music. Instead, Digital Factor revisits the production techniques, instruments, and sonic aesthetics that defined the decade, transforming them into a contemporary and distinctive sound. While many of the tracks subtly reference influential acts from that era, they never come across as derivative. I can hear echoes of Kraftwerk, Depeche Mode, and Fad Gadget, yet these influences are skillfully reinterpreted into an experimental form of Minimal-Electro that remains unmistakably Digital Factor. At first, “0.8” may not reveal all its strengths. It is not an immediately accessible album, but one that gradually draws the listener in and continues to surprise with its rich blend of influences and ideas. There are several outstanding tracks to discover here, making this, in my opinion, one of the strongest albums Digital Factor has ever released. The occasional female vocals add an extra layer of variety and elegance to the overall sound. “0.8” is likely to challenge listeners precisely because it refuses to fit neatly into a single niche. Yet that is also its greatest strength. Rather than reinventing itself completely, Digital Factor embraces innovation by reimagining the legacy of the 80s, resulting in an album that feels both nostalgic and strikingly forward-looking. (Rating:9). The album was preceded by the “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” EP, which served as its first preview. Listen to “Poor Mind”: Poor Mind by Digital Factor About Digital Factor Digital Factor started in Altenburg, Germany, in 1993. Formed by Mike Langer, Torsten Heise, and Tino Schmidt, the later line-up phases included Guido Litke and Leo von Leibnitz. Musically the project brings a mix of EBM and electro with later on also synth-pop, techno, and crossover elements. The first release was the 1994 Hard Records EP “F.A.L.L.I.N.G.-Down”. A move to Hyperium / Hypnobeat followed, bringing “Relationchips” in 1995, “On Demand” in 1996, “De Facto” and “Countercheck” in 1997, and “Over One Million Times” in 1999. After a quieter period, the band returned with “One More Piece” in 2006, “Look Back To Go Forward” in 2009, and “Trialog” in 2011. Alfa Matrix signed the band in 2020 and released “Come With Me”. That release was followed by “A Chemical Process” in 2021, a few back-catalogue reissues, the “What?” EP in 2022, and in 2023 the singles “I Am What I Am” and “Ouvre”, along with the charity album “G.B.A.-General Behavior Abrogate”. Gwendolyn Gaffa joined Mike Langer as a permanent studio and live member ahead of the “They Will Forget You (When You Die)” EP, released in April 2026 as the first preview of “0.8”, the full album reviewed here.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以八十年代新浪潮为概念基础，回收那个年代的制作技术、乐器配置与声音美学，将其转化为具有当代辨识度的实验性Minimal-Electro作品。乐评特别指出，虽然可以听到Kraftwerk、Depeche Mode、Fad Gadget等经典乐队的影响痕迹，但作品并未落入模仿窠臼，而是将这些元素融入独特的极简电子框架中。Gwendolyn Gaffa的正式加入为人声层增添变化与优雅感。专辑并非即时亲和型，而是需要时间逐步展开，多次聆听后仍能不断带来新发现，被视为该项目三十余年历程中最强的专辑之一。核心策略不是全面自我重塑，而是通过重新诠释八十年代遗产，达成既怀旧又向前看的平衡。

items.body: To understand why we're here—we writers, you readers, both listeners to this kind of music—requires skills that we, with a law degree, can't offer. Instead, we’d need to turn, depending on which School of Thought we’re referring to, to Freud or Lacan. What we could try to do is to share what drives us to buy certain records rather than others, excluding the dyschaolic compulsiveness that isn't ours. In short, we could say: 1) claiming to be completists of some musicians (try that with Mats Gustafsson and then tell us...); 2) a recommendation from a source (magazine, blog, fanzine, radio etc.) we trust; 3) the advice (damn, they're NEVER wrong...) from the FJC editors; 4) taking a leap into the void with an artist completely unknown to us, just to push away our personal horizon or, vice versa, 5) the need to breathe a little bit in our comfort zone, let’s say, with a reissue of Mingus or Taylor. There's reason number 6) for this review: to pay homage to an artist we love, in this case the Frenchman Michel Portal, who passed away at 90 last February. While Weather Report was never our cup of tea, we're not so obtuse as to fail to recognize the greatness of Miroslav Vitous, whose bio, from Chick Corea to Miles, is completely pointless to summarize, just as it is for Jack DeJohnette, honored on these pages on the occasion of his passing, in a way only this blog can do. We will always remember Portal as the author of that 1969 Our Meanings and Our Feelings , which represents to us one of the "6 Star Records" to be sent into hyperspace to make aware anyone who should find it of what free music means. His extraordinary artistic career has been enriched by collaborations with the likes of Boulez, Berio, and Stockhausen, which have defined his profile as a forward-looking musician, always respectful of History and Tradition. In our more than humble opinion, he remains a resoundingly underrated musician, so much so that, if memory serves, even our forum archives have no trace of him. Now you know. Ten years after his last album with ECM, as the label's liner notes tell us, Vitous creates with Mountain Call , a sort of musical self-portrait that demonstrates his immense talent as an improviser, composer and sampling pioneer. The album strikes a balance between spontaneous improvisation and sequences in which the recording studio's technology is put at the musicians' service, like a canvas on which to paint brand new soundscapes. Miroslav and Jack have not forgotten that they were one of the most thermonuclear rhythm sections ever and the rust of time has not affected their sublime class: “Tribal Dance”, “Epilog” and “Evolution” are there to demonstrate it incontrovertibly. The latter features Bob Mintzer's bass clarinet (Tito Puente, Buddy Rich, Art Blakey, Thad Jones, Jaco Pastorius, and Billy Cobham among his collaborations), while in the five-part suite "Rhapsody" we can hear Esperanza Spalding's vocals, making her ECM debut. The extraordinary bassist/vocalist joins Vitous, Gary Campbell's sax (on record with Randy Brecker, John Abercrombie, Dan Wall, Adam Nussbaum, among others), and Gerald Cleaver's drums (Sylvie Courvoisier, Charles Gayle, Roscoe Mitchell, Wadada Leo Smith, William Parker, Craig Taborn) on "Fun and Games," where "call and response" dynamics are inserted within the textures created by Vitous. The keystone, however, lies in the opening and closing of the album, which see Vitous and Portal perform astonishing duo sequences, probably the freest moments of the Czech bassist's artistic journey, since his collaboration with Jan Garbarek on "Atmos." Sheer beauty and irrepressible bliss, period. Anyway, forget the trivial and negligible considerations that drew us to this album and, whatever yours, if any, definitely give it a listen: this is a really relevant work that delivers much more than it promises. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是低音提琴大师米罗斯拉夫·维图斯、萨克斯演奏家米歇尔·波塔尔与鼓手杰克·德约内特三人的合作，延续了ECM厂牌近十年的酝酿。乐评以悼念波塔尔为契机展开，指出其曾与布勒兹、贝里奥、施托克豪森等当代古典巨匠合作，是一位被严重低估的前瞻性音乐家。专辑在自发即兴与录音室技术运用之间取得平衡，电子采样作为新音色画布服务于音乐表达。维图斯与德约内特曾是最具爆发力的节奏组合，时隔多年再度合作仍展现出惊人的默契与水准。评论特别提及五乐章组曲《Rhapsody》中出现了Esperanza Spalding的人声，以及《Evolution》中Bob Mintzer的低音单簧管演奏，凸显其跨领域合作网络。

items.body: Label: Shifting Paradigm Records, 2026 Personnel - Bryan Murray: tenor saxophone; Adam Linz: bass; Dan Monaghan: drums. Boasting a catchy sound and enjoying genuine freedom within the structure, saxophonist and composer Bryan Murray leads a supple chord-less jazz trio featuring bassist Adam Linz and longtime associate drummer Dan Monaghan. With friendship and collaboration at the center of Wolf , Murray—who also leads the peculiar avant-garde-meets-country band Bryan and the Haggards, is a member of Moppa Elliott’s Unspeakable Garbage, and has performed with David Byrne and St. Vincent outside the jazz sphere—explores his own music, radiating energy and abandon in a way that keeps listeners fully engaged. “ Bombs ” kicks off with hooky, motivic saxophone firepower over agile drums and sturdy bass, channeling David S. Ware and the reed language of Threadgill’s Air over the tight-knit rhythmic web spun by Linz and Monaghan. Post-bop and avant-garde walk hand in hand here, while “ Curtain ”, delivered with a sensitive balladic touch, brings forth Monaghan’s mallet work and shimmering cymbal washes. There’s pensive lyricism cutting through the open spaces, and Murray’s cautious melody is closely shadowed by Linz. Evoking childhood memories in West Virginia, “ Dirtslide ” displays an irreverent, hard-bop-inflected elegance over a full-throttle swing that is briefly suspended to accommodate the conversational interaction between Linz and Monaghan. Tactical bass mobility and crisp drumming dominate until Murray’s return, his playing abounding in ideas, supported by a firmly grounded and energetic rhythm section. The folksy theme of this piece contrasts with the pure modal jazz of “ Buell ”, a passionate prayer that recalls the spiritual hymns of John Coltrane and Billy Harper. “ Cloud Shapes ” is anchored by Linz’s impeccable bass guidance, while Monaghan’s cymbal work and mallets transport us to distant worlds. Murray’s narrative gift is unmistakable here. The title track, “ Wolf ”, achieves an air of mystery through a simple yet relentless bass ostinato. Deliberately measured, it unfolds in a lugubrious 3/4, while the closer, “ Fill Taker ”, embraces avant-garde elasticity, with Murray’s authoritative presence enhanced by well-delineated lines and motifs over a vibrant rhythmic foundation. This is stirring, serious sax-bass-drums work, resulting in a contemporary jazz album well worth digging into. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Bombs ► 03 - Dirtslide ► 05 - Buell ► 08 - Fill Taker
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由Bryan Murray领衔的无和弦乐器三重奏专辑，成员包括贝斯手Adam Linz与鼓手Dan Monaghan。专辑将后波普与先锋爵士并置，在结构内保持着充分的自由。穆雷的次中音萨克斯以钩子般的动机与旋律线条著称，在《Bombs》中展现出David S. Ware式的爆发力，在《Curtain》中则以细腻的抒情性延展。专辑也带有一定的地域叙事色彩，例如《Dirtslide》唤起了西弗吉尼亚的童年记忆。《Buell》以纯粹的调式爵士风格呼应了Coltrane与Billy Harper的灵性传统。Linz的低音线条扎实且富有策略性，Monaghan的钹与槌击技巧贯穿始终，构建出多层次的织体。标题曲《Wolf》以持续的低音固定音型在3/4拍中铺展神秘氛围，终曲《Fill Taker》则展现了先锋爵士的弹性张力。整体而言，这张唱片展现了当代爵士三重奏在自由与结构之间的精妙平衡。
