items.body: Talking Heads released their third studio album, “Fear of Music,” on 3 August 1979 through Sire Records. The album turns 47 this year. Produced by Brian Eno and the band, “Fear of Music” followed “More Songs About Buildings and Food” (1978) and preceded “Remain in Light” (1980), the middle record of three consecutive Eno collaborations that reshaped the band’s sound. Talking Heads recorded the album’s basic tracks on 22 April and 6 May 1979 at drummer Chris Frantz and bassist Tina Weymouth’s loft in Long Island City, Queens, using the Record Plant’s mobile studio, then completed the record at the Hit Factory, Atlantic Studios, RPM Studios and Record Plant in New York City. Greg Calbi mastered the album at Sterling Sound. The eleven-track album is sequenced across two sides: “I Zimbra,” “Mind,” “Paper,” “Cities,” “Life During Wartime” and “Memories Can’t Wait” open the record, followed by “Air,” “Heaven,” “Animals,” “Electric Guitar” and “Drugs.” King Crimson guitarist Robert Fripp guests on opener “I Zimbra,” whose lyrics set a Hugo Ball Dada poem to music. “Fear of Music” streams on Spotify. About Talking Heads Talking Heads formed in New York City in 1975. David Byrne and Chris Frantz had played together as the Artistics at the Rhode Island School of Design from 1973, joined by fellow student Tina Weymouth on bass after the trio moved to New York City in 1975. The band played its first show as Talking Heads on 5 June 1975, opening for the Ramones at CBGB. They signed to Sire Records in November 1976 and released their first single, “Love → Building on Fire,” in February 1977. Jerry Harrison, formerly of the Modern Lovers, joined on keyboards and guitar in March 1977, completing the lineup. The debut album “Talking Heads: 77” followed in 1977 and produced the single “Psycho Killer.” “More Songs About Buildings and Food” (1978) marked the band’s first collaboration with Brian Eno and included a cover of Al Green’s “Take Me to the River,” which became the group’s first Billboard Top 30 hit. “Fear of Music” (1979) continued the Eno partnership, mixing post-punk with funk and disco rhythms, and “Remain in Light” (1980) closed the trilogy with West African polyrhythms drawn from Fela Kuti’s music, which Eno had introduced to the band. Talking Heads reached its commercial peak in 1983 with “Speaking in Tongues” and the US Top 10 single “Burning Down the House.” The following tour was filmed by Jonathan Demme for the concert film “Stop Making Sense” (1984). “Little Creatures” (1985) became the band’s best-selling album, “True Stories” (1986) served as the soundtrack to Byrne’s film of the same name, and “Naked” (1988) became the group’s final studio album. Byrne left the band in 1991 and Talking Heads disbanded. The band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2002, reuniting briefly to perform. The 47th anniversary of “Fear of Music” places the album at the midpoint of Talking Heads’ three-album run with Eno, between “More Songs About Buildings and Food” and “Remain in Light.”

items._cn_summary: 本文为Talking Heads第三张录音室专辑《Fear of Music》发行47周年的纪念性介绍，属于资讯类文章而非深度乐评。文章罗列了专辑的录制信息、制作班底与曲目顺序，并概述了乐队从1975年组建至1980年代的简明发展史。音乐上，专辑由Brian Eno联合制作，混合后朋克的冷峻质感与放克、迪斯科节奏，开篇曲采用Hugo Ball的达达主义诗歌作为歌词，Robert Fripp担任客席吉他。整体处于新浪潮向世界音乐节拍过渡的阶段，与后续《Remain in Light》中的西非多节奏实验形成铺垫。

items.body: Alchera Vision has released the Castle Party 2026 compilation, a limited digiCD tied to the annual Castle Party festival at Bolków Castle, Poland. The release is out this week, on 7-8 August 2026. It comes in a 3-panel digipak with 19 tracks running 71 minutes, and is distributed in Europe through Audioglobe. Castle Party 2026 by Various Artists The “Castle Party 2026” compilation continues an annual series that Alchera Vision has produced alongside the festival since at least 2014, pairing festival headliners with newer acts and offering radio edits, remixes, video versions and tracks making their first appearance on CD. The 2026 edition mixes acts who played this year’s Bolków edition with others connected to the festival’s wider circle, spanning EBM, darkwave, gothic rock, post-punk and industrial styles. Castle Party 2026 compilation tracklist Empathy Test – “Monsters” (Radio Edit) – 04:00 Ash Code – “Nostalgia” – 03:13 A Projection – “No Control” – 03:02 Mayflower Madame – “A Foretold Ecstasy” – 04:36 Long Night – “Ghost” – 03:55 The Last Digital Angel – “One” – 02:38 Tribulation – “Drink The Love Of God” – 02:56 Merciful Nuns – “Elysene” – 03:19 Moonspell – “Opium” (Radio Edit) – 02:46 Agonised Too – “Lurking Fear” (Video Version) – 04:11 This Morn’ Omina – “(The) Rûach (of God)” [CCF] – 04:57 Rue Oberkampf – “Eternity” – 04:21 Denuit – “Wounded Heart” (Mila Dietrich Remix) – 03:00 Sierra Veins – “My Poison” – 03:27 Unter Null – “Coming Up To Breathe” – 05:32 Dawn Of Ashes – “Viral Decay” – 04:14 Hocico – “Hey Tú!” (with Prayers) – 04:12 Xotox – “Leben und Sterben für Musik aus Strom” (EXT!ZE Remix) – 03:33 She Pleasures Herself – “Last Goodbye” – 03:42 Several acts on the “Castle Party 2026” compilation played this year’s festival at Bolków, among them Empathy Test, Hocico, Denuit, A Projection, She Pleasures Herself, Long Night, This Morn’ Omina, Agonised Too and Rue Oberkampf. Sierra Veins, who also performed at the 2026 edition, contributes “My Poison” to the tracklist. About Castle Party Castle Party began on 20 August 1994 at Grodziec Castle, drawing around 300 people to see five Polish bands early in their careers: Moonlight, Daimonion, T.R.H., Pornografia and Fading Colours. The festival outgrew Grodziec within a few years and moved to Bolków Castle in 1997, the enclosed medieval courtyard setting it has kept since. Attendance grew from roughly 800 in 1995 to around 4,000 by 1999, when Clan of Xymox headlined. Castle Party became a three-day event in 2000, and its 2026 edition ran across four days, from 16 to 19 July, with a line-up including Moonspell, Diary of Dreams, Hocico, Empathy Test, Rotersand, Covenant and XOTOX across the Castle Stage and Park Stage. Side-Line covered the full 2026 timetable in May and published a four-day report from Bolków after the festival. Held annually at Bolków Castle in Poland, it is described as the biggest festival of its genre in Eastern Europe. About Alchera Vision Alchera Vision is the Polish label behind the annual Castle Party compilation series, releasing new editions to coincide with the festival and distributing them in Europe through Audioglobe. Its back catalogue includes prior “Castle Party” compilations dating back to at least 2014, alongside catalogue numbers such as the TRAITRS debut album “Rites and Ritual”, first released via the label in May 2017. The “Castle Party 2026” compilation extends that yearly series, again drawing its tracklist from artists connected to the festival’s line-up and circle.

items.body:
Since everyone else has written something about the centennials of Miles Davis and John Coltrane, why not join the parade? It is a good opportunity to look at the timeline of bassists the legendary trumpeter and saxophonist used. Born just under four months apart, the pair worked together under the elder Davis’ name periodically between Fall 1955 and Spring 1957 before a more steady affiliation in 1958-1960.

It is in that latter period that this analysis will begin, as it gives a convenient bit of serendipity: the fact that two of the their most famed albums were made in that period, Davis’ Kind Blue (March 2nd and April 22nd, 1959 for Columbia) and Coltrane’s Giant Steps (May 4th–5th and December 2nd, 1959). And the analysis will end with Coltrane’s death in 1967, which came during the tenure of Davis’ “second great quintet” and before his groups swelled and electrified during his fusion period.

As such, we begin with the same man, the bassist on both those albums: Paul Chambers. He had taken up the bass a decade earlier in his adopted home of Detroit (where he was a student at the seminal Cass Technical High School ... more on that later). He arrived in New York in 1954 at 19. By the time of Kind of Blue and Giant Steps, he had been on over 100 sessions from dozens of leaders, with multiple dates under Davis (with whom he had started working in late 1955) and Coltrane (who had used him for several albums in 1957-58 as well as both fellow sideman for many others and Chambers also hiring Coltrane for his own sessions). In addition to the five albums he led, Chambers played on sessions for Benny Golson, Curtis Fuller, J.J. Johnson, Lee Morgan, Red Garland, Sonny Clark, and Sonny Rollins.

The collaboration between Davis and Chambers was remarkably fruitful before and after Kind of Blue and solidified a part of Davis’ music that had previously seen widely differing players like Tommy Potter, Oscar Pettiford, Al McKibbon, and Percy Heath. The rest of 1959 saw multiple engagements around the country and closed with recordings that would be part of another monumental record, Sketches of Spain, that paired Davis’ group with the Gil Evans Orchestra. 1960 continued that momentum with more Sketches of Spain recording and almost non-stop touring, including two stretches in Europe, from Spring onward. 1961 and 1962 had more of the same activity, the documents being Someday My Prince Will Come and Quiet Nights. Then, quite suddenly, Chambers left Davis’ group in early February 1963.

It should be stated that Chambers did not restrict his activities solely to Davis, recording over four dozen albums during the period with, among many others, Jackie McLean, Wynton Kelly, Benny Golson, Hank Mobley, and Curtis Fuller. And after leaving Davis, he worked steadily with an array of leaders through the end of 1968, sadly passing away from tuberculosis caused and/or aggravated by drug abuse at only 33.

Stepping right into the Davis group was another Cass Technical High School alumnus: Ron Carter. Nearly 26, Carter was already prophesying his prolific career, participating in over three dozen albums since 1960, with the likes of Charli Persip, Yusef Lateef, Eric Dolphy, Don Ellis, Coleman Hawkins, Cecil Payne, Jaki Byard, Wes Montgomery, Bobby Timmons, Tadd Dameron, Dizzy Reece, Ken McIntyre, Milt Jackson, Benny Golson and others, plus waxing his leader debut, Where?, for Prestige subsidiary New Jazz in 1961.

It was Carter’s arrival that heralded Davis’ soon-to-be seminal band, though it took until Fall 1964 for its personnel to solidify. With Carter, Davis recorded Seven Steps To Heaven and played the Antibes festival in 1963. What is interesting though is while the “second great quintet” is thought of as a monolith, the bass chair had some upheaval/fluidity, depending on how you look at it. Gary Peacock – already a veteran and likely the only person to work for both Bud Shank and Albert Ayler – took the chair for nearly six weeks in the spring of 1964, Carter returning thereafter through the end of the year. 1965 began auspiciously with the January recording of E.S.P. but then things derailed with a convalescing Davis unable to play. And when he could, in November and December, Carter, a hot commodity, was absent, spelled by Peacock once more, then Reggie Workman, who had come up around the same time as Carter and had already come and gone in the groups of Coltrane. In 1966, Carter would return to the group but only partially, participating in East Coast performances, shows elsewhere having either Richard Davis, Carter’s only real equal in terms of fecundity, or in the Peacock mold of eclecticism, Eddie Gomez, returning permanently in October, just before the album Miles Smiles. 1967 was similar: Carter was on board when not busy elsewhere, Gomez on call, then Albert Stinson for one show (a little over two years before his passing – see Bass Tragedies column in Issue 94) and then another veteran, Buster Williams, for a tour (and playing on one track of the 1981-released compilation album Directions). Carter would fill a fixed point for all of 1967, including the albums Sorcerer and Nefertiti and would continue with Davis through the middle of 1968.

Like Chambers or perhaps even more so, Carter was also on the greater jazz scene during his tenure with Davis. He recorded on sessions led by his fellow Davis bandmates but also by everyone from Bobby Timmons, Charles Lloyd, Donald Byrd and Bobby Hutcherson to Jimmy Smith, Shirley Scott, Eddie Harris, and Stanley Turrentine, to name only a handful. He has, of course, gone on to be likely the most recorded bassist in jazz history.

Paul Chambers’ time under Coltrane was shorter and more intermittent. After Giant Steps he was part of, along with the rest of Davis’ period band, November 1959 recordings that would partly comprise Coltrane Jazz and be brought back 18 months later as one of three individual bassists taking part in the Africa/Brass recordings (though his contribution was only heard on the 1995 complete sessions version).

Also in 1959 was a Birdland engagement for Coltrane where either Ahmed Abdul-Malik or George Tucker, both established and close in age to Coltrane, were on bass.

In 1960 Coltrane hired the slightly younger Steve Davis in what seems to be his first professional engagement. Davis stayed in the band through the end of the year for all its live dates and played on music recorded in October and released piecemeal on My Favorite Things, Coltrane Jazz, Coltrane Plays the Blues, and Coltrane’s Sound. Though Davis lived until 1987, his credits after Coltrane were slight: the Mangione Brothers, Dave Burns, McCoy Tyner, Kenny Dorham, James Moody, Freddie McCoy, and Eddie Jefferson, all made in the ‘60s. One deviation in the year came via Coltrane’s shared date with Don Cherry, The Avant-Garde, where bass was handled by either Charlie Haden or Percy Heath.

1961 was a year in flux, bassist-wise, for Coltrane. He introduced a concept to which he would return later in the decade by using two bassists for an engagement at Chicago’s Sutherland Lounge in March: Raphael Don Garrett and Workman, the former, about six years younger, working with Roland Kirk, Paul Serrano, and Eddie Harris, the latter 11 years younger, sideman for Gigi Gryce, Donald Byrd, Duke Jordan, Richard Williams, and Dave Pike.

Workman would be part of the aforementioned Africa/Brass, as would, separately, another bassist, Art Davis, already with credits under Max Roach, Lee Morgan, Booker Little, Hal Mooney, Ernestine Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie, Leo Wright, Clifford Jordan/Sonny Red, Abbey Lincoln, and Booker Little. But in May they were together for Ole Coltrane and nearly a month at the Village Vanguard in August. Workman would become the fixed bassist for Coltrane through the end of the year for concerts, including a European tour, and a small portion of the Ballads album from the end of the year. An exception was Workman either alternating or alongside Jimmy Garrison for a November stint at the Village Vanguard.

If not for a family health crisis forcing Workman to leave the group at the end of 1961 and return to his native Philadelphia, he likely would have stayed with the band and jazz history been quite different. It should be said that Workman hardly is a footnote, becoming one of the most revered players of his generation. But it was Garrison who became the anchor. Born between Garrett and Workman, prior to joining Coltrane he had worked with Philly Joe Jones, Curtis Fuller, Kenny Dorham, Jackie McLean, JR Montrose, Walter Bishop, Jr., Ornette Coleman, Bill Barron, and Ted Curson.

Unlike Carter and Davis, once Garrison was on board, he stayed there. That was mostly to do with Coltrane’s packed schedule of touring and albums and that, unlike Davis, he was healthy and non-combustible. From 1962-1964, Garrison was omnipresent, including the bulk of Ballads, Duke Ellington & John Coltrane (where he split duties with Ellington’s period bassist Aaron Bell), 2018 discovery Both Directions At Once, John Coltrane And Johnny Hartman, Impressions, Crescent, another new millennium unearthed gem in Blue World, and closing out the year with Coltrane’s magnum opus A Love Supreme (which added Art Davis for a second day of recording, released as a second disc to the album’s deluxe edition in 2002).

In 1965 Garrison was still the main man but occasionally Davis would be alongside him: partially on The John Coltrane Quartet Plays in February and fully for June’s Ascension. Otherwise, Garrison was the sole bassist for performances and most of the other albums: Transition, Sun Ship, and Meditations. The exceptions without Davis were overdubs of Haden for the posthumously released Infinity and Garrett returning to play both bass and clarinet for Live In Seattle (as well as the 2021 archival release A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle), Om, and part of Kulu Se Mama.

1966 was even more Garrison-centric, with the only documented work including a second bassist shows in November and December with Lionel “Sonny” Johnson, the brother of Dewey Johnson, who had played on Ascension. The last year of Coltrane’s life, Garrison was there as well, with one notable absence: the Coltrane/Rashied Ali duet Interstellar Space.

Unlike Chambers or Carter, Garrison was kept so busy during his time with Coltrane that his outside discography at the time is meager, though it does include his sole leader date, Illumination! with the Elvin Jones/Jimmy Garrison Sextet. Otherwise it was sessions with Lorez Alexandria, Coltrane bandmate McCoy Tyner, Sonny Rollins, Bill Dixon, and Robert F. Pozar.

After Coltrane’s death, Garrison kept working but his documentation slowed, his two Blue Note dates with the Jones trio rounded out by Joe Farrell being the most enduring. There were also dates with Rolf and Joachim Kuhn, Clifford Thornton and Nathan Davis, and regular work with Alice Coltrane and Archie Shepp. His final recording came in early 1975 with Beaver Harris and Dave Burrell’s 360 Degree Music Experience. Garrison died of lung cancer in 1976 at 42.

items.body:
The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items._cn_summary: 这是芬兰手风琴演奏家玛丽亚·卡拉涅米与钢琴家蒂莫·阿拉科蒂拉合作35年后的专辑《Morgondimma》。整张作品以二重奏为核心，偶尔加入弦乐四重奏扩展音色。手风琴旋律抒情甜美，钢琴则以克制而精准的方式支撑并丰富音乐层次。两人默契深厚，能够在无谱状态下展开无缝即兴。除传统曲目外，还收入了原创作品以及皮亚佐拉的探戈曲，体现出北欧民谣与南美探戈的微妙交汇。整体气质安静流畅，呈现出梦幻般的聆听质感，不追求炫技，而是以服务旋律为旨。乐评指出这张专辑虽不会引发轰动，却提供了纯粹的听觉之美。对偏好实验、前卫与即兴的听众而言，这是一张温馨但偏向传统语境的北欧室内民谣作品，跨界幅度有限。

items.body:
LOCAL（国内）
NEWS
河合孝治著「マンガでわかる現代音楽入門〜世界は最初から鳴っていた」刊行
2026年8月5日
編集部

マンガで分かる！音楽は出来事だ。世界は最初から鳴っていた。読みながら、音楽の常識がひっくり返る。音楽にお未来をひらく、思考の旅へ。ケージ、即興、身体、AI、サウンドアートまで。クラシックの限界、偶然性、即興、身体表現、AIまでーー20世紀以降の音楽の革命をマンガと図解でやさしく解説。
著者。河合孝治氏の熱い想いがいろんなキャッチフレーズで表紙に踊る著作『マンガでわかる現代音楽入門〜世界は最初から鳴っていた』(TPAF) が刊行された。
河合は慶應義塾大〜同大学院〜日本大学大学院芸術学研究科音楽芸術専攻修了の履歴を持つサウンドアーチスト、コンセプター。音楽を中心に様々なアート、身体表現、哲学、仏教などをクロッシングしながら電子音楽やビジュアル・アートの制作、ピアノの即興演奏、学際芸術研究 (芸術と西洋哲学・仏教思想）を行っている。特に影響を受けたものとして、ジョン・ケージ、タージマハール旅行団の音楽、ナム・ジュン・パイク、荒川修作のアート、ショーペンハウアー、ニーチェの生の哲学、デリダやドゥルーズなどのポストモダンの思想、そして華厳、唯識、中論などの仏教思想を挙げている。
本書では、ジョン・ケージと彼の作品＜4分33秒＞、ケージに決定的な影響を与えた鈴木大拙の禅思想をベースに「音楽とは何か？」「聴くとは何か？」が現代音楽を理解するための基本として語られる。９章を通してマンガ（AI生成と思われる）で問題提起と解説が行われ、次いで図解とテキストで確認作業が行われる。基本は何度も繰り返され、読み進むうちに既成概念が解きほぐされ著者の思想世界に誘導される仕組み。著者は自らパフォーマーであり実践を通した解説は説得力に富む。
発行元は著者が主催する TPAF (https://tpafart.com) 定価：￥2,100＋税

items._genre: contemporary classical / experimental / improvisation / sound art
items._cn_summary: 本文为河合孝治著作《マンガでわかる現代音楽入門》的出版新闻稿，介绍其以漫画形式解说二十世纪以降现代音乐革命的入门书。书中以约翰·凯奇及其《4分33秒》为起点，结合铃木大拙禅思想，探讨"音乐是什么"与"聆听是什么"的命题，涉及偶然性、即兴、身体表现、AI、声音艺术等主题。全文由九章构成，以AI生成漫画进行问题提出与解说，再以图解与文本进行确认，引导读者进入作者融合电子音乐、钢琴即兴、哲学与佛教思想的跨领域艺术世界。作者身兼创作者与研究者双重身份，从自身实践出发提供解说。文章主体为书讯发布而非乐评，对音乐作品的听觉内容着墨甚少，无法作为有效的音乐评论参考。

items.body: Birmingham MC Admiral Jerry, born Jerry Butler, cut “Up and Coming MC” and “Demonstrate” with UB40 in 1985. He is back with “Chant Down Babylon”, out on Windrush Day, 22 June, the date the HMT Empire Windrush docked at Tilbury in 1948. Butler grew up in Handsworth, a first-generation Black Briton of Jamaican heritage. Grammar school and a private education came next. The racism did not. “Growing up in Handsworth as a first-generation Black Briton, I experienced plenty of racist attitudes at grammar school and throughout my education,” he says. “This song is for oppressed people everywhere who are hoping and striving for a better tomorrow.“ The lyrics name Kunta Kinte, George Floyd and the Windrush Generation. Jerry works the riddim as a toaster, chatting across a roots reggae backing in the old sound system manner. Aldo Dice produced the track at his Farda Dice Studios in Birmingham for The Empire Windrush EP, with Sovereign Tugz and See No Equal on the mix and master. Jah Mission, the Amsterdam production house, shot the video across Birmingham and London. It settles on the Benjamin Zephaniah mural in Handsworth Park, unveiled in honour of the poet and activist on Windrush Day in 2024, the year after his death. More music from Jerry arrives in early 2027. Stream “Chant Down Babylon” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Admiral Jerry – Chant Down Babylon appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Last Friday, Nottingham's Beyond Grace released the third and final installment in their Welcome to the New Dark Ages series, an EP trilogy set to hit the shelves physically as a full-length album later this year. Andrew Walmsley, Ed Gorrod, Tim Yearsley, and Chris Morely have been working on this technical death metal saga since November 2023, releasing each segment independently and intermittently amongst a stable output of singles. Just under a year after part one, its sequel came out, and this July, the line concludes. Welcome to the Dark Ages. Part III tracks the formula of the previous releases: three songs per extended play, with a total runtime of thirteen to fourteen minutes, hosting universally reliable death metal.Part III, acting as the ceremonial effort, should be the episode listened to first to get the freshest taste of the band. Guest vocalist Bethany "Beef" Pitts of social justice thrash collective Transgressive lends the opening track, "Radium Angels," a mean, modern attitude and pairs nicely with softer cleans and metallic instrumentation. Following that, deathcore vibes radiate from "Reign of Error," mainly coming from the slow, yet not-over-the-top breakdown. "First As Tragedy" completes the recording with another short and sweet offering.Part II and Part I follow suit in solidity, with Part II tapping deeper into proggy rhythms and moodier atmospheres, and I displaying an edgier version of Beyond Grace, prone to experimentation and evolution. If you crave three small, back-to-back injections of nice English metal totalling no longer than a regular LP, Hey! Listen to Beyond Grace!
items._genre: technical death metal / death metal / progressive metal
items._cn_summary: 这是英国诺丁汉乐队Beyond Grace发行的三部曲EP系列的最终篇章，三首曲目共十三至十四分钟，属于技术死亡金属范畴。评论将其作为入门推荐，第三部作品延续前作框架，开篇曲与客座主唱贝瑟尼·皮茨合作呈现出带有现代态度的硬核节奏，中段曲目散发着死亡核式的慢速breakdown，末曲短小精悍。第二部深入探索前卫节奏与阴郁氛围，第一部则展示乐队更具实验性的进化面貌。整体定位为英国本土的技术死亡金属，结构紧凑，适合寻求短小金属冲击的听众。

items.body:
Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

items.body: In August 1819, tens of thousands of working men and women gathered in St. Peter�s Field in Manchester to hear the politician Henry Hunt speak. They were difficult times, many still out of work after the Napoleonic wars, rising prices and low wages � and always those at the bottom of the heap suffering. Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. Further reading: The Young'uns - Tiny Notes (Review) Ben Nicholls - Duets

items.body: A "groovy, mid-tempo style known for its exaggerated bouncy rhythm and common pornographic themes” is RateYourMusic’s general description for pornogrind. An offshoot of goregrind, pornogrind is not much more than what you just read. As a microgenre, it takes the already off-putting genre of goregrind (death metal-meets-grindcore-meets-preversion), and further integrates intense sexual and violent themes, a majority of the time both. I grew up with virtually zero internet supervision: on the off-chance one device was taken away, I’d resort to YouTube'ing music on any other means possible: even my Nintendo 3DS. I remember when even that was confiscated after rather suggestive rap music videos littered my search history. My time as a late teenager in the metal field—predominantly as a reviewer—has certainly built my character and provided me with some outstanding campfire tales, as I’ve seen things most anyone would never want or need to, ever. This ranges from adult content of various extremities to, to a significantly lesser extent, gore. Faintly, I recall stumbling across famous clips of violent movies, coincidentally right before bedtime. This bleeds into my experiences with pornogrind, or whenever I’m shipped a promo of a grind record, as it always results in temporary prayer to whoever’s in charge that the gore–no matter how explicit it may be–is illustrated. That gore I can tolerate, because at least it’s not genuine. Most metalheads have unfortunately stumbled across Mayhem’s infamous live album cover depicting the vivid aftermath of lead vocalist Dead’s suicide. Hell, I’ve seen it plastered on black Gildan t-shirts on TikTok. Images like these will always irk me harder than any, say, Cannibal Corpse cover, because at least theirs is illustrated. Yes, I’m not thrilled about seeing dead fetuses strung up by meat hooks or corpses mid-fellatio, but I reiterate, at least it’s illustrated. My appreciation may even flourish if it's allegorical, artistically evocative, or inventive in a way of an original presentation of the macabre. This is exactly why progressive metal is my rendezvous genre, as colorful, modern demonstrations (see Voyager - Colour in the Sun or ERRA - Silence Outlives the Earth) are, besides philosophical or literary subjects, the norm. I can waste hours leafing through progressive metal album covers without fear of scarring myself, and this practice is directly rooted in my time with progressive rock, a genre that took my younger teen years in a chokehold. Fantastical, sprawling landscapes, all hand-drawn by talented virtuosos . Alas, relating to the topical genres, goregrind is brimming with bare-bones, graphic photography, often medical (band names most likely named after whatever operation is depicted), and other gory shit, but pornogrind is where the boundaries once thought to be immovable hit the unstoppable object. In preparation for this issue, I want to elucidate that I do not solely devote my time to sifting through these albums and their covers, nor if I were to, would I relish it. My prefrontal cortex has already molded through phases unknown, and I'm sure in no time it will again.Pornogrind’s birth began with Gut, a Germanic group that blended death metal with grindcore-length bouts of brutality and incredibly reprobate ideas. Their 1991 demo tape, Drowning in Female Excrements, is credited as the first pornogrind release, and their first longplay, Odour of Torture, picturing a woman using her breast as a pin cushion (yeowch!), is the premier pornogrind album, signed to a one-man label named Regurgitated Semen Records (a one-man label still active, currently supporting five bands). No, I haven’t listened to it, and I most likely never will. Thirty-nine tracks, forty-four minutes: time I’ll dedicate to other metal projects not concerning “Triple Penetration” or “The Taboo Room.” Their ski mask-clad appearance acted as a foundation for the physical aesthetics of the acts taking part in pornogrind, and it’s not surprising that patrons often shield their faces–their digital footprint can always be traced. Since Gut’s heyday, RateYourMusic has catalogued 803 pornogrind releases, Gut being the mainstay for the next two chronologically. The highest-rated album on RateYourMusic for the genre is our good friend Gut’s 2020 LP Disciples of Smut, receiving a 3.42/5 from 262 ratings. Another well-renowned website, AOTY (Album of the Year), ranks the same: Disciples of Smut, with a 75/100 from twenty-five ratings. I can see why this record is comparably prevalent: the artwork, considering the genre, is rather tame; a black-and-white, crust-punk-ish display with a decrease but not abstinence, in pornographic visuals. The record’s material is also supposedly watered down by standard death and black metal influences, rendering it accessible to the broader metal community. Sadly, my morbid curiosity and thirst for knowledge took the best of me, and I ultimately caved and glanced at the top ten records of the genre. Thankfully, it’s fairly safe to do, and there are a couple of positive visual surprises. The second “greatest” pornogrind record is from Czechia’s Carnal Diafragma, unorthodoxly titled Space Symphony Around Us. The cover? Asteroids crossing a reddish planetary body. One of the songs is “The Art of Nature.” Carnal Diafragma clearly defies the conventional visual standards of their style, but after a quick audio sample, their music sounds exactly like any other pornoband. Another interesting item is Plasma, which takes the bronze medal. They present a vintage comic-book style interpretation of The Tarantula’s movie poster for their 2007 release Creeping! Crushing! Crawling!. The juxtaposition of graphic novel styling with music that is both graphic and novel is an interesting observation, but nonetheless unsurprising. Moving onwards, the seventh spot goes to Rompeprop from the Netherlands with another colorful comic book impression with Gargle Cummics. The most eminent band on the list is Gutalax, which gained immense social media traction for the singer's screechy vocals and (I cannot believe I’m saying this) comparably safe-for-work, scat-themed music videos. Europe dominates in this field per metal standards: The Nordics propagate the darkest and bleakest of black metal, central Europe brings the best out of power metal, and the entirety of the North birthed the lucious melodies of symphonic metal. It seems it also produces, like any other continent, a fair share of utter garbage.So that was lovely, but the real reason why you haven’t heard of this microgenre up until now is that it’s actively fading away. The only time it really reached actual reporting was after the 2019 Dayton shooting, in which the culprit was the lead singer of a short-lived collective called Menstrual Munchies. The headline is only somewhat sensationalist, giving the audience, who probably don't listen to metal at all, a vivid taste of what pornogrind is truly about. One of the bandmates took the initiative and took all the recordings of the band, claiming that "whereas I saw it as a joke...he didn't," and further commenting that he "doesn't want to be associated with [the band]." The article also supplies an efficient abstract on the genre, covering much of the material I came across. This incident actually provoked Rolling Stone, the world's most pedestrian music magazine, to remark on the style, referencing Gut, Slipknot (yes, members of Slipknot momentarily played in a little collective titled Anal Blast/Anal of Blast), before turning the topic to gun control.Still, the fade is only a positive. By succinct, self-censored scanning, it takes no decrypter to conclude that pornogrind is misogynistic as hell. A majority of the imagery and lyrical topics are insanely degrading towards women. While the devil's advocates will browbeat me about how “shock value is shock value,” I peck right back and ask them where their morals stand. The sheer amount of unexplainable online animosity directed towards women in general should be distasteful for any metalhead. Gratefully, online music databases show quite a minute amount of 2026 pornogrind releases, a considerable cut displaying anime girls in downright despicable situations or genuinely incomprehensible visual nonsense. A majority of these recordings appear to be low quality and not worth anyone’s time. It seems that each year, the pace of production of p-grind is deteriorating, and this is partially due to influential critics reciprocating my qualms by labeling the genre as “juvenile” and “straight from the toilet.” Even Metallum, the internet's largest metal music repository, doesn't officially recognize p-grind as a genre, instead filing any affiliated group under goregrind with pornographic lyricism. Metallum, admittedly, is infamous for its questionable rules of acceptance and ability to determine if a band is actually metal (for example, Rush is accepted, yet Between the Buried and Me isn't, on account of not being "metal enough"). Still, any website ready to ignore p-grind is a smidge more credible in my view. So, I've concluded the point of why p-grind isn't an appealing genre, but why has there been such a stark decline in activity? The most reasonable explanation is the convolutedness of the microgenre's concept. I love labeling music as much as the next nerd, but as I established earlier, p-grind retains little sonic originality compared to its stylistic parent. To my trained ear, the two genres sound exceptionally identical to the point where if you played two songs (this trial would only take a minute or two, thanks to the brevity of the material), I would have a rough time discerning the two. Why would band A want to distance itself from band B if both A and B are so similar? If A is goregrind with porn-themed writing, which is already a common choice in the genre, yet doesn't explicitly label itself as the likes of B, which labels itself as strict p-grind, then who, when it comes to pure material, cares? It's a matter of labeling, and if we keep to this trend of creating new styles, the soon-to-be micromicrogenres will only pertain to one or two groups. Shit, frognoise is a thing, and it's nothing more than heavy grind with amphibian content. If I go listen to, say, TrollfesT's "Dance like a Pink Flamingo," am I listening to folk metal, or flamingo metal? It's almost natural selection nowadays, when p-grind molds back into goregrind. The band with the third-highest-rated p-grind record, Jig-Ai, slowly morphed back into regular grind after their 2006 self-titled effort. Many bands follow this pipeline, so does this signal that every p-grind band will eventually technically cease?Another culprit towards the category's decline is the blatant laziness radiating from the partakers. Take Girlcock, a Quebecois p-grind project that operates under AI-generated album covers, or Pepeka Massacre, a Brazilian entity that thrives on laughably awful NSFW cartoons, exemplifying the low effort that these artists put forth. I'm yet to hear something convincing come from the genre, because the riff-forward nature and terseness of pace limit the amount of genuine distinctness a p-grind record can produce. Surely I'm not claiming some of the instrumentalists that thrive under p-grind aren't talented, but a lot of them are clearly using this genre to effortlessly MIDI their way into the metal sphere. GarageBand is an app pre-installed on most iPhones, toyed with momentarily by most new phone users, then discarded moments later to free space. Making p-grind is shockingly easy to do on this app, and little knowledge in production is needed for one to churn out record after record on an app like this and flood online databases, inflating the album count. This doesn't actually happen, of course, as, by assumption and pattern recognition, people lazy enough to make their music this way aren't exuding much effort to log in their presence on music databases.Let us all rejoice this year that pornogrind is slowly fading into obscurity. I’ve seen enough literal and metaphorical alien things shoved into other things for the rest of my life, thank you.

items.body:
For years, Picheolin has lived comfortably as one of SEVENTEEN's most beloved recurring characters — a "nosy, yet kindhearted ahjussi" whose comedic charm has endeared him to CARATs. In 吉BOARD, however, DINO asks a different question: What happens when the character steps out of the skit and into an album of his own?

The answer unfolds across seven tracks that revisit different generations of Korean music. Rather than feeling like a collection of nostalgic experiments, 吉BOARD gradually builds a musical identity for Picheolin — one that's playful, heartfelt and unmistakably him. And in doing so, the album also offers a glimpse of DINO — not behind Picheolin, but through him.

To mark the release of 吉BOARD, Bandwagon spoke with DINO about transforming Picheolin into a fully realised musical persona and the experience of creating his first solo project.

Your previous solo releases, including ‘Wait’ and ‘Trigger’, have shown different sides of you as DINO. For your first solo album, however, you chose to step into a beloved and familiar character, Picheolin. What made you feel that this was the right character – and the right moment – to build an album around?

I spent a lot of time asking myself what I could offer that no one else could. Ultimately, Picheolin became my way of bringing a fresh style both sonically and visually, as well as a platform connecting people across generations.

Picheolin has existed for several years, but creating an album around him requires building not just a character, but a musical identity as well. How did you begin translating his personality into the sound of 吉BOARD?

I wanted to pack this album with Picheolin’s playful charm, humor, and philosophy on life. Far beyond lighthearted fun, my hope was to infuse the music with Han* (the bittersweet emotional depth) and Eol* (unbroken spirit) at the heart of Korean culture, creating a festive chaos where everyone can connect.

*Han: A uniquely Korean sentiment encompassing deep sorrow, resilience, and an underlying hope.

*Eol: The collective spirit, soul, and shared consciousness that forms the core identity of the Korean people.

“I usually have a lot on my mind and reflect deeply on life, but Picheolin feels like a space where all those thoughts naturally turn into something much more intuitive, warm, and playfully honest.

Picheolin may have started as a character, but 吉BOARD is ultimately still a body of work created and performed by you. In what ways does Picheolin reflect who you are as DINO, and what has creating music through him allowed you to express that you might not have otherwise?

I’d love for listeners to pay close attention to the lyrics of 吉BOARD. While we all live different lives, I believe the core emotions we feel aren’t all that different. Picheolin gave me the freedom to express those raw, honest stories in a much more unfiltered way. And because I was very involved in the entire songwriting and production process, every part of this album is naturally infused with who I truly am.

吉BOARD moves across several generations of Korean music, from sounds rooted in the past to ones much closer to the present. What drew you to revisit those different eras, and what made them meaningful to both Picheolin's story and your own journey as an artist?

First, I really wanted to capture the full spectrum of life’s joys and sorrows, which led me to concepts that best fit each of those emotions. As taking on my first solo EP was a major challenge, it brought me a deep sense of responsibility—one that I’ll carry with me as I look ahead to my next album as DINO.

The album marks DINO's first solo EP, but it also builds on years of creating within one of K-pop's most successful self-producing groups. Working alongside longtime SEVENTEEN collaborator BUMZU while welcoming new collaborators such as HITCHHIKER and DEUX's Lee Hyun-do, DINO carried the same collaborative mindset that has long defined SEVENTEEN into every stage of the album's creation.

SEVENTEEN has always been known for its collaborative approach to music. What lessons did you carry into 吉BOARD from working with the members, and how did they react when they heard the album?

For me, it really comes down to the importance of communication. What matters most is staying connected with everyone involved to incorporate each perspective, whether from the artist or the songwriter. That’s why I made sure to have open discussions throughout the entire process.

What stuck with me most was just how warmly the members responded. Seeing them vibe so naturally with each track was amazing, and their encouragement to trust myself and stay confident gave me a real boost.

You've grown up alongside SEVENTEEN, and you're now entering a new chapter as a solo artist. Looking ahead to the group's 13th anniversary, what do you hope you'll have discovered about yourself as an artist by then?

Above all, I want to bring out my strengths to their fullest potential. For me, that means uncovering my untapped musical colors and sharing stories that feel completely and uniquely my own.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SEVENTEEN (@saythename_17)

“We all have different tastes when it comes to what’s cool, but my hope for this album is that it brings a sense of freshness and opens up a new perspective for everyone who listens.”

While 吉BOARD introduces listeners to another side of Picheolin, it also quietly marks the beginning of DINO's own journey as a solo artist. Across seven tracks that celebrate life's small joys, lingering heartaches and everything in between, the album never dwells in one emotional space for too long. Whether it's the infectious exuberance of ‘Party Rock Rock’ or the wistful longing of ‘Love Sick’, 吉BOARD ultimately feels like music people can celebrate, laugh with, and find comfort in — long after the songs themselves have ended.

One last question — this time for Picheolin himself. If you had to personally sell someone a copy of 吉BOARD on the street, what would your sales pitch be?

Youngsters, older folks, and kiddos—gather ‘round~ Give this album a spin and follow my lead! Now… 사랑의 눈빛! (Eyes of love!) 😎

items.body:
Ivoris is taking her music across Asia! The singer-songwriter and producer has announced the Pour My Heart Out 2026 Asia Tour, which will see her perform in Hong Kong, Taipei, Singapore, Bangkok, and Manila this October in support of her forthcoming album, Pour My Heart Out, due out this September.

The newly announced run follows the success of Ivoris' sold-out China tour, which played five cities, including her biggest headline show to date in Guangzhou. Before heading across Asia, the artist will also embark on her third headline tour across China this August.

Fans can expect a setlist featuring brand-new songs from Pour My Heart Out alongside favourites such as 'Drive Thru' and 'I Wish My Mind Would Shut Up'. Each stop on the tour will also feature a special guest, while concertgoers will have the chance to purchase exclusive hand-designed merchandise created by Ivoris herself.

Designed to bring Ivoris' dreamy pop and R&B world to life, the shows promise a mix of soaring pop anthems and intimate acoustic moments. Speaking on the announcement, the artist shared, "I've been dreaming about bringing this album to the world, and it's finally happening. I can't wait to pour my heart out at these shows and sing and dance with everyone."

The announcement comes at a milestone moment for Ivoris, whose music has continued to gain momentum across Asia. Since debuting in 2018, she has built a growing international audience with her introspective songwriting and ethereal sound, amassing more than 222,000 monthly Spotify listeners and millions of streams worldwide.

Pour My Heart Out 2026 Asia Tour dates:

9 October — Hong Kong — MoM Livehouse

12 October — Taipei — The Wall Live House

14 October — Singapore — ATP Live House

15 October — Bangkok — Blueprint Livehouse

17 October — Manila — Teatrino Promenade

Fans can signs up for the pre-sale here. Tickets for the Asia tour will be available tomorrow for Hong Kong, Taipei, Singapore, Bangkok and Manila.

items.body:
For decades, Andrew Chow, better known as DJ Wiz, helped define what hip-hop and R&B sounded like in Singapore’s clubs. A champion turntablist, influential resident DJ and generous mentor, his impact travelled far beyond the booth, reaching the DJs, dancers and club-goers who grew up around the scenes he helped build.

Chow died on 3 August at the age of 63. His daughter, Abby Bernadette Chow, announced the passing of her “dearest Daddy” in a Facebook post, thanking friends and fans for the messages that had poured in for him.

“I am glad to see all the sweet and touching messages and tributes to him,” she wrote. “He passed on peacefully and he would be so happy to know that you guys appreciate him so deeply.”

According to The Straits Times, Chow died of stomach cancer. He remained connected to Singapore’s DJ community in the final months of his life, appearing as a judge and performer at the DMC Warm-Up Battle at Kossa on 24 May.

The tributes that followed his death spoke to a legacy much larger than a list of championships or club residencies. Chow was remembered as a teacher, a brother, an inspiration and, for the dancers who spent their nights beneath his booth, a DJ who always seemed to know how to make a room move.

The sound of a night at Phuture

For many, Chow will forever be associated with Phuture, the room within Zouk where his sets became part of the rhythm of Singapore nightlife. He was the kind of resident DJ who did more than soundtrack a night. By introducing audiences to unfamiliar records, transforming favourites through his turntablist technique and reading the mood of the floor, he helped shape the identity of the space itself.

Zouk opened in March 1991 and became instrumental in bringing international club culture to Singapore. Phuture followed in December 1996, taking over the former MTV Bar and initially offering downtempo music, drum & bass, breakbeats and ambient sounds alongside the main club’s house-focused programming.

As Phuture evolved, it became one of the city’s defining homes for hip-hop and R&B. Chow, who had become part of Zouk’s DJ roster during the mid-1990s, was central to that identity, developing a reputation for sets that crossed old-school hip-hop, R&B, funk, soul, rock, big beat and breaks without losing their sense of direction.

Chow moved effortlessly between slower grooves and harder, more energetic selections, weaving elaborate scratches and swift transformations into sets that felt both technically precise and instinctively attuned to the dance floor.

That balance was what made Chow such an enduring resident. A battle DJ could impress through precision, speed and dexterity, but a club resident had to build an entire evening, responding to the people in the room while guiding them somewhere they did not necessarily expect to go. Chow could do both, making difficult techniques sound effortless while keeping the dance floor at the centre of the experience.

His scratches did not feel like demonstrations inserted into a set. They became part of the music’s momentum — an accent before a drop, a burst of tension between songs or a sharp reminder that the person behind the decks was actively reshaping the records in real time. For regulars, a night at Phuture was not only about hearing the songs they loved; it was about hearing what Chow could do with them.

A champion who never lost sight of the crowd

Chow was a three-time DMC Singapore champion and won the Singapore leg of the Technics World DJ Championships in 1998. Those victories established him as one of the country’s leading turntablists during an era when the craft required years of physical practice, close listening and an intimate understanding of vinyl.

By the late 1990s, an archival newspaper profile was already presenting DJ Wiz as an experienced fixture in the scene. His rise coincided with a period when DJs were increasingly being recognised not only as people who selected records, but as musicians and performers capable of manipulating sound with their hands.

Scratching, beat juggling and rapid transformations brought a new physicality to hip-hop DJing. A skilled turntablist could isolate a fragment of sound, repeat it, cut it apart and rebuild it into something entirely new, often using little more than two turntables, a mixer and an exact sense of timing.

Chow had the control to thrive in that world, but his importance came from how naturally he carried those techniques into the club. He did not treat turntablism as something that belonged only in competitions or specialist showcases. Through his residencies, he placed the craft in front of mainstream audiences who might never have attended a battle but could immediately feel its effect on the dance floor.

His work showed that scratching did not have to interrupt a party. It could serve the rhythm, heighten anticipation and turn the transition between two records into a performance of its own. In Chow’s hands, technical mastery and crowd awareness were not opposing skills; they strengthened each other.

That ability made him an important bridge between two versions of the DJ: the competitor judged on precision and originality, and the resident entrusted with the emotional journey of a room. His titles confirmed what he could do behind the decks, but the loyalty of generations of club-goers revealed why it mattered.

Chow later became an in-house DJ at Kyo, extending a career that had already made him one of Singapore’s most recognisable figures in nightlife. As venues, formats and musical trends changed, he remained grounded in the fundamentals of selection, timing and knowing when a crowd was ready to follow.

Passing the craft forward

Some DJs leave behind recordings and memorable sets. Others leave behind students, protégés and entire networks of people who carry their knowledge into new rooms. Chow did both.

In 2001, he was teaching at AudioSports DJ Academy, where students could learn the technical foundations of the craft. An archival feature on the school identified DJ Wiz as both Zouk’s resident DJ and an instructor, placing him within one of the spaces where a younger generation first gained structured access to professional DJ techniques.

His role as an educator is crucial to understanding the scale of his impact. Singapore’s DJ community did not grow only through major clubs, international bookings or high-profile competitions. It also grew through lessons, practice sessions, equipment demonstrations, shared records and the informal passing down of knowledge from one practitioner to another.

Chow was part of that infrastructure. He had spent years mastering the details of phrasing, timing, scratching and mixing, but he did not keep that expertise to himself. By teaching, mentoring and sharing what he knew, he helped lower the barriers for younger DJs trying to find their own place in the scene.

Teaching DJing involves more than explaining how to use equipment. It means training someone to listen for the structure of a song, recognise the moment when two records can meet and develop the confidence to make decisions while an audience is watching. Chow helped younger DJs build those instincts, and his influence continued whenever one of them stepped into a booth or passed the craft on again.

Where the DJs met the dancers

Chow’s role in Singapore’s hip-hop story also extended beyond the DJ community. His years at Phuture placed him in direct conversation with the dancers, breakers and crews who gathered around the music he played.

According to Radikal Forze’s account of its history, Chow helped spark the formation of Radikal Forze after watching b-boys dancing during his nights at Phuture in 1998. While the collective’s complete origin story belongs to the dancers who formed and developed it, the account reflects how closely Chow’s booth was connected to the movement happening on the floor below.

That relationship captures what a club such as Phuture could become at its best. The DJ and the dancers were not operating in separate worlds. Breakers responded to the drums, breaks and rhythms coming from the speakers, while their movement encouraged DJs to search for records that could challenge them, energise a cypher or keep the exchange alive.

Chow stood at the centre of that conversation. He was not simply playing hip-hop to a passive audience; he was helping create the conditions in which a community could form around it. The records became meeting points, connecting people who might later build crews, organise events, teach others and shape Singapore’s wider hip-hop culture.

His influence therefore cannot be measured only through the number of people who watched him perform. It also lives in the relationships that began in those rooms, in the dancers who found one another through the music and in the communities that continued growing after the lights came on.

From competitor to custodian

As Singapore’s turntablism scene developed, Chow’s role evolved. He remained a performer, but he also became one of the veterans entrusted with recognising and encouraging the next generation.

By then, he had moved from champion to mentor, and from resident to custodian of the culture. His presence connected a new generation of DJs to a history built through vinyl, mixers, record bags, repeated practice and the patience needed to master a physical craft.

Chow continued performing across Singapore’s nightlife circuit, appearing at Phuture celebrations, ZoukOut and a multitude of notable bars and clubs around the country. These bookings were more than exercises in nostalgia. His sets allowed different eras of club music to meet, showing how records from the past could still create an immediate response in the present.

He belonged to a generation that experienced several major changes in DJ technology, from vinyl and early digital systems to contemporary software and controllers. Yet equipment was never the defining feature of his performances. What endured was his ear, his touch and his understanding of how to turn individual songs into a shared experience.

“He was a teacher and a brother”

Chow’s final public engagement brought him back to the competitive culture that had helped establish his name. At the DMC Warm-Up Battle on 24 May, he performed and served as a judge despite having been unwell, remaining present in the community he had spent decades nurturing.

He was also due to receive the DMC Legacy Award at DMC Singapore, scheduled to take place at RASA on 6 September. According to The Straits Times, the award was intended to recognise his lasting contribution to Singapore’s turntablism and DJ culture.

Following his death, the people who had worked beside him and learnt from him remembered both the performer and the person behind the decks. KoFlow spoke of a legacy that would continue through the DJs and turntablists Chow had influenced and helped cultivate.

Kavan Spruyt, the founder of RASA, remembered watching Chow command Phuture and described him as “invincible during his prime”. DJ Small, whose real name is Eddie Chan, remembered him as “a teacher and a brother”, praising his deep musical knowledge and his ability to mix and scratch across genres.

Those tributes revealed how Chow’s technical reputation was inseparable from his generosity. He was admired for what he could do, but loved for how willingly he shared it — through formal lessons, quiet encouragement, nights spent performing beside younger DJs and the example he set each time he approached the decks.

Abby’s statement gave those memories their most personal frame. Her words were not about trophies, residencies or status. They were about how happy her father would have been to know how deeply people appreciated him.

That appreciation is the real measure of Andrew Chow’s career. It can be found in the DJs he taught, the turntablists he inspired, the dancers who gathered beneath his booth and the club-goers who still remember the precise moment when one of his mixes changed the energy of an entire room.

For some, the memory will be of a scratch cutting sharply through the speakers. For others, it will be a familiar record arriving at exactly the right moment, or the sight of a packed Phuture dance floor responding as one.

Chow helped show Singapore that DJing could be several things at once: a technical discipline, a performance, a profession and a way of bringing people together. The music eventually had to stop, but what he set in motion did not.

items.body:
Red Velvet are back just in time for the season with the release of their new mini album, Velvet Summer, alongside the music video for its breezy title track, 'Surfin' Boy'.

Velvet Summer marks the group's first full-group comeback since 2024's Cosmic. The five-track record sees Red Velvet embrace a softer, more mature take on their signature summer sound, weaving together bossa nova, reggae, dance-pop, classical, and acoustic influences while highlighting the quintet's signature versatility.

Leading the release is 'Surfin' Boy', a laid-back dance-pop track built around mellow bossa nova guitar, relaxed reggae rhythms, and a polished house groove. Paired with the group's dreamy harmonies, the song captures the carefree feeling of drifting across the ocean on a sunny day. JOY also penned the lyrics for both 'Surfin' Boy' and album track 'Hawaii', adding a personal touch to the mini album.

Ahead of the release, Red Velvet reunited with fans at the sold-out 2026 Red Velvet FAN-CON, held from 31 July to 2 August at Korea University's Hwajeong Gymnasium in Seoul. Fans were treated to the first live performances of both 'Surfin' Boy' and 'Hula Hoop' before the album officially dropped.

Known for beloved seasonal hits including 'Red Flavor', 'Power Up', 'Umpah Umpah', and 'Queendom', Red Velvet continue to expand their legacy as one of K-pop's defining summer acts. With Velvet Summer, the group revisits the bright energy fans know and love while introducing a more refined and understated sonic palette.

items.body:
Fans of Girls Band Cry are in for a treat as TOGENASHI TOGEARI are finally heading to Singapore for their first-ever performance in the country.

The Japanese band will take the stage for a one-night-only concert on 19 August at Capitol Theatre, bringing their TOGENASHI TOGEARI "Rinne no Kotowari" SOUTHEAST ASIA TOUR 2026 to local fans.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SOZO LIVE (@sozoasia)

Formed through an audition organised by agehasprings, TOGENASHI TOGEARI is the real-life band behind the original anime series Girls Band Cry. Beyond voicing the anime's main characters, the members perform its opening, ending, and insert songs while maintaining an active live career.

Following the anime's broadcast debut, the band's momentum grew rapidly as every one of their theme songs entered Spotify's Viral Chart, making them one of the rare rookie acts to have five songs chart simultaneously. They also reached another milestone with their solo performance at Nippon Budokan in September 2025. Their music is produced by acclaimed producer Kenji Tamai.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SOZO LIVE (@sozoasia)

Fans should note that the touring lineup will feature Rina, Yuri, and Shuri. Members Mirei and Natsu are currently on hiatus and will not be participating in the Southeast Asia tour.

DAYOUNG has joined forces with Jay Park for the first time on their new collaboration single, 'FLIRTY'. The upbeat pop track explores the excitement and uncertainty of new romance, capturing the quiet anticipation before two people become something more.

Blending warm guitar melodies with groovy rhythms, 'FLIRTY' fuses contemporary pop with touches of R&B and reggaeton. The single pairs DAYOUNG's bright, polished vocals with Jay Park's laid-back delivery, creating a dynamic that reflects two perspectives on the early stages of attraction.

The collaboration arrives as DAYOUNG continues to build on the momentum of her solo career following the release of her debut single album, gonna love me, right?, which featured the breakout title track 'body'. Since making her solo debut, the WJSN member has earned her first music show win and established a distinct performance-focused identity outside of the group.

'FLIRTY' also marks a new creative milestone for the singer, expanding her musical range through her first-ever collaboration with Jay Park while continuing her evolution as one of K-pop's rising soloists.

BABYMONSTER have transformed into vampires for the music video of their latest track, ‘MOON’.

The cinematic visual sees the group step into a dark horror-fantasy world beneath a blood-red full moon. The members awaken inside coffins, reveal sharpened fangs, transform into bats, and take on high-flying action sequences while dressed in striking black-and-red looks.

The music video quickly rose to No. 1 on YouTube’s Worldwide Trending chart following its release.

‘MOON’ appears on BABYMONSTER’s third mini album, CHOOM. It concludes the group’s three-month visual project, which also featured music videos for ‘CHOOM’, ‘SUGAR HONEY ICE TEA’, and ‘I LIKE IT’.

A performance video for ‘MOON’ is set to arrive on 5 August at midnight. According to YG Entertainment, its choreography will feature movements inspired by the moon and the track’s chorus lyric, “I’m the moon.”

items.body:
Maroon 5 are heading back to Asia. The three-time GRAMMY Award-winning band have unveiled the Asian leg of their international tour, bringing their arena show to fans across the region in early 2027.

The run follows performances across Latin America and North America, as well as headline appearances at Hyde Park in London and Rock in Rio, with the band continuing to support their latest album, Love Is Like. Fans can also expect to hear the group's newest single, 'Heroine', alongside a catalogue of career-spanning hits.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation Asia (@livenationasia)

The 2027 Asia tour will make stops in:

24 January — Kaohsiung, Kaohsiung National Stadium

27 January — Seoul, KINTEX Hall 4 & 5

30 January — Tokyo Dome

31 January — Tokyo Dome

2 February — Tokyo Dome

5 February — Jakarta, Jakarta International Stadium

7 February — Manila, SM Mall of Asia Arena

9 February — Bangkok, Impact Arena

12 February — Singapore, National Stadium

As the official payment partner for the Asia tour, Visa will offer eligible cardholders early access to tickets and exclusive fan experiences across selected markets. Visa presales begin on 12 August for Singapore and Kaohsiung, 13 August for Manila, and 19 August for Bangkok. Click here for more ticketing information.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

The tour will wrap up in Singapore, where Maroon 5 are set to perform at the National Stadium on 12 February 2027. Tickets will go on sale from 14 August, following a series of presales.

Singapore ticket details:

Artist Presale: 11 August, 10 AM – 11:59 PM

Visa Presale: 12 August, 10 AM – 13 August, 10 AM

Live Nation Presale: 13 August, 12 PM – 11:59 PM

General Sale: 14 August, 10 AM

items.body:
Travis Japan have released ‘On My Road - Stadium ver. -’, a reworked version of their fan-favourite track built for bigger stages and even bigger singalongs.

The digital single expands on the warmth and optimism of the original with a more sweeping, crowd-ready arrangement.

‘On My Road’ first appeared on the standard edition of the group’s second single, KAGENIMO-HINATANIMO. The track centres on gratitude, resilience, and moving forward with the people who have supported Travis Japan along the way.

The release arrives as the seven-member group continue to grow their presence outside Japan. It also follows the premiere of their Disney+ docuseries, which sees them embark on a 10-day road trip across the United States and return to Los Angeles, where they spent time together before their debut.

Travis Japan were also appointed the inaugural J.League 2026/27 Season Special Ambassadors. They are scheduled to perform ‘On My Road’ during halftime of the Meiji Yasuda J1 League opening match between Yokohama F. Marinos and Kashima Antlers at MUFG Stadium on 7 August.

The song will also feature in the season’s J.League television commercial, DAZN broadcasts, and football programming across Japan.

Its accompanying music video was filmed inside a stadium and follows the members as they perform across the venue before coming together at centre field. As lights rise from the grass around them, the stadium transforms into a dreamlike setting that reflects the song’s hopeful message.

items.excerpt: Psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder: Perspective from meta-analysis - PubMedThis meta-analysis indicates that standard-dose psilocybin mapubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov タイトル Psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder: Perspective from meta-analysis （日本語訳：大うつ病性障害に対するシロシビン補助療法：メタ解析からの視点）著者 Taro Kishi（岸太郎）、Kenji Sakuma（佐久間健二）、Masakazu Hatano（波多野将一）、Hiroyuki Uchida（内田裕之）、Nakao Iwata（岩田仲生）ら掲載誌 Journal of Affective Disorders（感情障害学雑誌） 2026年8月1日発行（電子公開：2026年3月22日） DOI: 10.10
items.body: Psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder: Perspective from meta-analysis - PubMedThis meta-analysis indicates that standard-dose psilocybin mapubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov タイトル Psilocybin-assisted therapy for major depressive disorder: Perspective from meta-analysis （日本語訳：大うつ病性障害に対するシロシビン補助療法：メタ解析からの視点）著者 Taro Kishi（岸太郎）、Kenji Sakuma（佐久間健二）、Masakazu Hatano（波多野将一）、Hiroyuki Uchida（内田裕之）、Nakao Iwata（岩田仲生）ら掲載誌 Journal of Affective Disorders（感情障害学雑誌） 2026年8月1日発行（電子公開：2026年3月22日） DOI: 10.1016/j.jad.2026.121675 PMID: 41876058これは6件のランダム化比較試験（RCT）を対象とした系統的レビューとメタ解析で、大うつ病性障害（MDD）に対するシロシビン治療の有効性と安全性の時間的変化を調べた研究です。アブストラクトの正確な日本語訳目的 6件のランダム化比較試験を対象としたこの系統的レビューとメタ解析は、大うつ病性障害（MDD）に対するシロシビン治療の有効性と安全性の時間的変化を調べることを目的とした。方法 標準用量のシロシビン（1回あたり25 mg、または体重70 kgあたり20～30 mg）と低用量のシロシビン（1回あたり10 mg、または体重70 kgあたり15.05 mg）のサブグループごとに、別々にメタ解析を実施した。対照条件はプラセボ、待機リスト対照、ナイアシン、またはシロシビン1 mgであった。結果 標準用量のシロシビンは、うつ症状の軽減において対照群より優れていた（標準化平均差［SMD］：−1.05；95%信頼区間［CI］：−1.60 ～ −0.50、p = 0.0002、I² = 75%、K = 4）。待機リスト対照を含む研究を除外した感度分析では、かなりの異質性を伴わずに標準用量シロシビンの優越性が支持された（SMD：−0.70；95% CI：−1.03 ～ −0.36、p < 0.0001、I² = 43%、K = 2）。この感度分析には、マニュアル化されたシロシビン補助精神療法を組み込んだ2件の二重盲検試験が含まれていた。対照群と比較して、標準用量シロシビンは治療後2～3週時点での反応率（リスク比［RR］：2.34；95% CI：1.52–3.60、p = 0.0001、I² = 0%）および寛解率（RR：3.38；95% CI：1.88–6.08、p < 0.0001、I² = 0%）が高く、治療後6～12週時点での反応率も高かった（RR：2.61；95% CI：1.45–4.71、p = 0.001、I² = 0%）。さらに、標準用量シロシビンは対照群に比べてあらゆる理由による中止率が低かった（RR：0.39；95% CI：0.18–0.87、p = 0.02、I² = 0%）。標準用量シロシビンは、治療後1～9日以内の頭痛（RR：2.06；95% CI：1.11–3.81、p = 0.02、I² = 57%）および悪心（RR：10.20；95% CI：3.80–27.39、p < 0.0001、I² = 0%）の発生率が高かったが、これらの症状はこの期間を過ぎると消失した。低用量シロシビンは、対照群と比較して優越した有効性を示さなかった。 このメタ解析は、標準用量のシロシビンがMDD治療の有望な選択肢となり得ることを示している。しかしながら、今後の研究では、現行の試験間に存在するかなりの方法論的異質性に対処する必要がある。キーワード Depression（うつ病）、Meta-analysis（メタ解析）、Psilocybin（シロシビン）、Randomized controlled trial（ランダム化比較試験）、Systematic review（系統的レビュー）続きをみる

items.body: 2026.08.04 室内楽の魅力を一日で味わう特別な音楽祭から、夜公演をレポート 「室内楽の環 音楽祭」が7月20日、銀座・王子ホールで初開催されました。夜公演は初来日のヴァイオリニスト、エリック・シルバーガーとブラント・フレドリクセン（ピアノ）によるデュオ・リサイタル。世界初演を含む公演の模様をレポートします。 取材・文 取材・文 伊熊よし子 音楽ジャーナリスト・音楽評論家 東京音楽大学卒業。レコード会社勤務、ピアノ専門誌「ショパン」編集長を経てフリーに。クラシック音楽をより幅広い人々に聴いてほしいとの考えから、音楽専門誌に限らず、新聞、... 詳しく見る 「昼に出会い、夜に感動が極まる一日」と題した「室内楽の環 音楽祭2026」が7月20日に銀座・王子ホールで開催された。昼公演は弦楽四重奏、公開レッスン、トランペットソロ、ピアノ五重奏から六重奏まで多彩なプログラムが組まれ、初めて室内楽を聴く人に向けてモーツァルトからジョン・ウィリアムズの作品まで紹介され、公開レッスンではどのように室内楽が作られていくのか、そのプロセスが体験できるという手法である。 夜のデュオ・リサイタルは、ヴァイオリンのエリック・シルバーガーとピアノのブラント・フレドリクセンの登場。シルバーガーは第14回チャイコフスキー国際コンクールおよび2011年マイケル・ヒル国際ヴァイオリン・コンクール入賞者としてアメリカ国内外で幅広く活躍。使用楽器は1757年製ジョヴァンニ・バッティスタ・グァダニーニ。フレドリクセンはジュリアード音楽院ムンツ賞を受賞し、舞台作品の音楽監督を務めたり教育者としても活躍している。プログラムはモーツァルト、フォーレ、R.シュトラウスのヴァイオリン・ソナタと、ウィリアム・ワイゲルの《ヴァイオリンとピアノのための3つの対話》世界初演が組まれ、作曲家のワイゲルも客席で演奏を聴き、終演後はステージで挨拶を行なった。 シルバーガーのヴァイオリンは音量豊かで、その名器を朗々と響かせ、ピアノとのコミュニケーションを図る。一方、フレドリクセンの自由闊達なピアニズムもまた弦と合わせる極意を披露するものだった。とりわけ印象的だったのはワイゲルの世界初演の作品で、解説書に綴られた作曲家の文によると、「ヴァイオリンとピアノが対等な立場で語り合うことを大切にした」とのこと。冒頭の長く引き伸ばされた「ソ」の音が幾重にも変容して何度も登場する様子が印象的だった。そのワイゲルが編曲した「さくら」がアンコールで奏され、日本の美が新たな面を見せ、のびやかな変奏がコンサートの終わりを色彩感豊かに飾った。 公演情報 「室内楽の環 音楽祭」【夜公演】 エリック・シルバーガー & ブラント・フレドリクセン デュオ・リサイタル 日時：2026年7月20日 会場：王子ホール 曲目 モーツァルト：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ 変ロ長調 K.454 フォーレ：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ 第1番 イ長調 作品13 ワイゲル：ヴァイオリンとピアノのための3つの対話 世界初演 リヒャルト・シュトラウス：ヴァイオリン・ソナタ 変ホ長調 作品18
